decisions.title: Should Jet ship an official core.raylib graphics package (FFI-bridge pattern) for cross-platform games and visual demos?
decisions.gist: No first-party graphics package exists in Jet today. Raylib is a C library covering 2D/3D rendering, input, audio, and windowing across Windows, macOS, Linux, and web. The proposal is an official FFI-bridge package (not in the compiler) that gives Jet programs a clean native-graphics story for games, tools, and flagship demos.
decisions.explainer: The FFI-bridge pattern is already established in stdlib (Archive.rs, Db.rs, FFI.rs) — a package emits bridge template text without adding a crate to the compiler's Cargo.toml (I6-safe). Raylib is MIT-licensed, actively maintained, and purpose-built for exactly this use case. A first-party package signals intent and ensures the bridge is idiomatic Jet (markers, error types, safe wrappers). Without it, the only graphics path is user-authored FFI glue — not something beginners can do. This is also a flagship vertical: a working Jet game demo is one of the highest-signal proofs the language is real. The package lives outside the compiler; a community package would be acceptable if the community existed, but it doesn't yet.
decisions.story: I want to build a small game in Jet to learn the language. Every other modern language has a tutorial path to a moving sprite on screen. Jet has nothing — I'd have to write my own C FFI bindings to even open a window. An official raylib package makes 'write a game in Jet' a realistic first project.

options.name: Official core.raylib FFI-bridge package (recommended)
options.detail: Create a first-party package under the jet.* namespace using the FFI-bridge pattern (emits bridge template text; no Cargo.toml change in the compiler). Covers Window, Texture, draw, input, audio at minimum. Raylib is a native dep (C library) — sourced via nixpkgs on Nix; bundled raylib source fallback for non-Nix (raylib supports being compiled from source with no system deps). This is a package, not a Core module — opt-in only.

options.name: Leave to community packages
options.detail: Don't maintain a first-party raylib binding. Wait for community contributors to publish one. Tradeoff: the community doesn't exist yet; this leaves graphics entirely unaddressed for the foreseeable future. No flagship demo is possible without it. Not recommended while the ecosystem is empty.
options.code:
-- hypothetical community package (doesn't exist):
-- [dependencies]
-- raylib-jet = "0.1"  -- community-maintained, unknown quality

options.name: Plan an own renderer for later, nothing now
options.detail: Defer graphics entirely; plan a native Jet renderer (WebGPU or similar) as a future milestone. Tradeoff: a native renderer is a multi-year project; leaving graphics unaddressed now means no demos, no games, no visual flagship for years. The FFI bridge to raylib can coexist with a future native renderer — this option is false economy.
options.code:
-- no graphics today; future milestone:
-- core.gfx (WebGPU-backed, post-v1)

comparisons.note: Odin ships vendor:raylib as a first-party vendor binding in the standard distribution. It is consistently cited as a reason developers try Odin for game prototyping. The binding is idiomatic Odin, not raw C.
raylib-zig is an official community package. Less tightly integrated than Odin's vendor binding but widely used for Zig game tutorials.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a prelude opt-out directive, and/or let libraries mark names as prelude-injectable?
decisions.gist: The prelude auto-imports `print`, `input`, and a curated set. Two new ideas: (1) a user directive to opt out of the prelude, and (2) a library marker that puts names into scope without a prefix (`#builtin`-style). These can ship independently. This card decides both.
decisions.explainer: Opt-out lets expert users who want explicit imports take full control — a clean I1-compatible escape hatch. Library no-prefix injection is the riskier half: it lets any package pollute the default namespace, violates I8 (arbitrary second paths to a name), and defeats the prelude's curation. A library using this would look like Jet's own prelude to a beginner who can't tell the difference. Interactions: prelude `print`/`input` are ratified; this doesn't touch them. The `#builtin` marker is unratified scratch.
decisions.story: I'm writing a CLI tool with explicit imports everywhere for clarity. I want to put `#NoPrelude` at the top of my file and have zero implicit names — then import exactly what I use.

options.name: Opt-out directive only — no library injection
options.detail: Add a `#NoPrelude` file-level marker that disables auto-imports. Library no-prefix injection is declined (I8 violation — lets packages create arbitrary implicit paths). This is the minimal, safe escape hatch.

options.name: Both opt-out and library injection
options.detail: Libraries can mark exports with a `#Prelude`-style marker to inject names into callers' scope. Powerful but breaks I8 and the namespace contract — any dep can now shadow prelude names.

options.name: Neither — no changes
options.detail: Keep the current curated prelude with no opt-out. Expert users import on top of the prelude; the prelude names are always present. Simplest surface, least flexible.

comparisons.note: Rust offers `#![no_implicit_prelude]` for expert files while preventing dependencies from injecting names into every scope.
comparisons.code: #![no_implicit_prelude]

comparisons.note: `#![no_std]` and `#![no_implicit_prelude]` opt out of std and prelude respectively. Expert escape hatch, not the default.
`{-# LANGUAGE NoImplicitPrelude #-}` disables the Prelude import per-file. Libraries then re-export curated sets (Protolude, Relude).
comparisons.code:
{-# LANGUAGE NoImplicitPrelude #-}
import Protolude

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust offers `#![no_implicit_prelude]` for expert files while preventing dependencies from injecting names into every scope.
decisions.recommendation: Add opt-out only. This matches the best expert escape hatch while preserving Jet’s curated beginner prelude and blocking package namespace pollution.

decisions.title: Should Jet add an arbitrary-precision integer type (BigInt) to the standard library?
decisions.gist: No arbitrary-precision integer exists in Jet today. Fixed-width integers overflow silently in some contexts or trap. The question is whether to add a `BigInt` type — and if so, whether fixed integers auto-promote on overflow or whether BigInt is always explicit.
decisions.explainer: Sized integers are ratified (dsg9). The main design fork is overflow behavior: auto-promotion on overflow (Python model) vs explicit `BigInt` construction only. Auto-promotion is ergonomic but breaks the type: the return type of `+` on `Int` would depend on the value, not the type — incompatible with Jet's static type system. Explicit-only is the only safe fit. This also touches the decimal-money card: financial math may prefer `Decimal` over `BigInt` for exact representation. Interaction with I6: a BigInt implementation in std would use a Rust dependency unless native-implemented; owner approval required for any new I6 dep.
decisions.story: I'm computing a large factorial for a cryptographic key length check. The result doesn't fit in `Int64`. I want to write `BigInt(n).factorial()` and get the exact answer, not a wrapped or trapping result.

options.name: Core `BigInt` — explicit construction, no auto-promotion
options.detail: Add `BigInt` as a stdlib type. Fixed integers never auto-promote: `Int64 + Int64` stays `Int64` (traps or wraps per mode). BigInt is constructed explicitly. Fits static typing and I8.

options.name: Package-level only — not in core std
options.detail: BigInt ships as a first-party package (`core.math.bigint`), not in core. Keeps std small; user opts in. Suitable if demand is narrow (crypto, scientific). Same explicit-only overflow contract.
options.code:
import core.math.bigint.BigInt

let x = BigInt(2).pow(BigInt(128))

options.name: Defer — decide after decimal-money card
options.detail: The decimal-money card may clarify which exact-numeric niche BigInt fills vs Decimal. Deferring avoids shipping two overlapping numeric escape hatches.
options.code: // no BigInt yet

comparisons.note: Java `BigInteger` is standard, explicit, and never changes fixed-int overflow semantics by surprise.
comparisons.code: BigInteger x = BigInteger.TWO.pow(256);

comparisons.note: Int auto-promotes to arbitrary precision on overflow. Ergonomic but makes integer type semantics value-dependent — not viable in a static type system.
comparisons.code: x = 2 ** 1000  # plain int, arbitrary precision automatically

comparisons.note: `BigInteger` is a standard library class, always explicit. Fixed ints overflow without promotion. Closest model to option A.
comparisons.code:
BigInteger x = BigInteger.TWO.pow(256);
BigInteger y = x.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(99999999L));

comparisons.note: No BigInt in stdlib. `Foundation` has none either. Third-party `BigInt` package required. Matches option B.
comparisons.code:
import BigInt  // third-party
let x = BigInt(2).power(256)

decisions.bestCurrent: Java: Java `BigInteger` is standard, explicit, and never changes fixed-int overflow semantics by surprise.
decisions.recommendation: Add explicit core `BigInt`, no auto-promotion. Jet gets exact integers without making `Int + Int` value-dependent.

decisions.title: Should Jet ship grapheme-cluster iteration and Unicode normalization in the core standard library?
decisions.gist: Jet strings are Unicode-aware, but no grapheme-cluster iterator or normalization (NFC/NFD) API exists. Without these, user-facing text operations (length by visible character, string comparison) are incorrect for many languages. This is a new std API decision.
decisions.explainer: Grapheme clusters and normalization are distinct: you can ship iteration without normalization. Both require Unicode Character Database (UCD) tables, which are large (~1MB). Bundling in core std means every Jet binary carries this data; package-level avoids that for users who don't need it. The UCD tables must come from somewhere — a verified Rust crate via the FFI-bridge pattern is I6-compatible with owner sign-off, or native tables generated at build time. Interaction with native-deps memory: UCD is data, not a C lib, so the FFI-bridge pattern fits cleanly.
decisions.story: I'm building a text editor. I split the user's string on characters and the emoji with a skin-tone modifier counts as two — the cursor jumps wrong. I need `str.graphemes()` to iterate by visible cluster, not by codepoint.

options.name: Core: grapheme iterator + normalization (NFC/NFD)
options.detail: Both APIs ship in core std. UCD tables included in std via FFI-bridge or native. Binary size increases ~1MB. Correctness for user-facing text is a correctness concern, not an optional nicety.

options.name: Package-level (`core.text.unicode`) — not in core
options.detail: Both APIs ship as a first-party package. Core strings remain lightweight. Users who need correct text processing opt in. Avoids mandatory UCD bloat for CLI tools, network code, etc.

options.name: Grapheme iteration only — defer normalization
options.detail: Ship grapheme iteration in core or package; defer normalization (NFC/NFD) to a later card. The two are independently useful and can ship in sequence.
options.code:
for g in s.graphemes() { ... }  // iteration ships
// normalization deferred

comparisons.note: Strings index by extended grapheme clusters by default. `String.unicodeScalars` gives codepoint access. Normalization via `String.decomposedStringWithCompatibilityMapping`.
comparisons.code:
let s = "caf\u{E9}"
print(s.count)  // 4, grapheme clusters
let nfc = s.precomposedStringWithCanonicalMapping

comparisons.note: No grapheme iteration in std. The `unicode-segmentation` crate provides it. Normalization via `unicode-normalization` crate. Both are explicit opt-in.
comparisons.code:
use unicode_segmentation::UnicodeSegmentation;
for g in s.graphemes(true) { ... }

comparisons.note: No grapheme iteration in stdlib. Third-party `grapheme` package or `unicodedata` for normalization only.
comparisons.code:
import unicodedata
nfc = unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s)

decisions.title: Which compression codecs should ship with core library, and how — alongside or separate from archive containers?
decisions.gist: `core.archive` is the planned/in-progress archive container work (zip/tar). Compression codecs (gzip, zstd, brotli) are independent of archive containers — you can compress a stream without building a zip. This decides which codecs ship, where they live, and how they're sourced.
decisions.explainer: Archive containers and compression codecs are separate concerns: tar is a container, gzip is a codec, and a `.tar.gz` is both layered. Conflating them delays codecs behind archive work. The sourcing question is I6-relevant: gzip and zstd have well-maintained pure-Rust implementations; brotli is slower to stabilize. The FFI-bridge pattern (emit bridge template, don't add to jet Cargo.toml) is the I6-safe path for any Rust dep that needs owner sign-off. gzip and zstd are needed now (HTTP, network transfer, database wire formats); brotli is mostly web-server-side.
decisions.story: I'm writing a log aggregator that reads `.log.gz` files and writes compressed output to an S3-compatible endpoint. I need gzip decompress on read and zstd compress on write — I don't need to build a zip file.

options.name: gzip + zstd in std now; brotli later
options.detail: Ship gzip and zstd as `core.compress.*` in std via FFI-bridge. brotli is deferred to a follow-on card. These two cover the dominant use cases (HTTP, database, log files). Each requires an I6 sign-off per dep.

options.name: All codecs as packages — nothing in core std
options.detail: gzip, zstd, brotli all ship as first-party packages users opt into. Keeps std minimal. Adds friction for common tasks that most applications need.

options.name: Archive-only — defer standalone codec API
options.detail: Ship only what `core.archive` needs internally. No standalone `compress`/`decompress` API. Users who need codec-only access are blocked until a future card.

comparisons.note: `gzip`, `zlib`, `bz2`, `lzma` are in stdlib. `zstd` is third-party. Normalization of common codecs in std is the Python/Go model.
comparisons.code:
import gzip
with gzip.open('file.gz', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()

comparisons.note: `compress/gzip`, `compress/zlib`, `compress/flate` in std. zstd is a third-party package. gzip being in std is the clear expectation.
comparisons.code:
import "compress/gzip"
r, _ := gzip.NewReader(f)
io.Copy(os.Stdout, r)

decisions.title: Design the crypto envelope for algorithm agility now so PQ primitives can slot in later?
decisions.gist: The planned misuse-resistant crypto envelope (not yet shipped) will pick concrete algorithms. If we hard-code classical X25519 now, adding ML-KEM later means a breaking API change. The question is whether to design the envelope's internal seam for algorithm agility from the start, so hybrid X25519+ML-KEM can be wired in without user-visible changes when the primitives are ready. This is New/far-horizon and sequences after the crypto envelope card.
decisions.explainer: Algorithm agility means the envelope type carries an opaque algorithm identifier; the user picks a security tier (`#Classic`, `#Hybrid`, `#PostQuantum`) not a raw algorithm name — the implementation swaps the primitive behind the tag. This blocks on the crypto envelope card being decided first; don't implement either until that card lands. Blast radius: internal to the crypto stdlib module — no user-facing syntax change beyond the tier tags. Interacts with I6 (ML-KEM needs a vetted crate or native implementation, both require owner approval). NIST finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in 2024; X25519+ML-KEM-768 is the IETF hybrid draft.
decisions.story: I'm deploying a long-lived service today. I want to know that when post-quantum key exchange is ready, I change one tag and recompile — not rewrite my protocol layer.

options.name: Agility seam now, PQ algorithms later
options.detail: Design the envelope API with an opaque algorithm tier (`#Classic`, `#Hybrid`, `#PostQuantum`) rather than exposing raw algorithm names. Ship classical only; ML-KEM slots in when ready. User call sites never change. Requires sequencing after the crypto envelope card.

options.name: Classical only for v1, revisit later
options.detail: Ship the envelope with X25519 hard-coded. Defer agility design until PQ is actually needed. Risk: API break when PQ lands. Safe for near-term; technical debt for services with long key lifetimes.

options.name: Defer entirely
options.detail: Don't decide until the crypto envelope card is resolved. Keeps this off the plate; revisit as part of that card's follow-up.
options.code: // no crypto envelope yet; defer both

comparisons.note: Modern TLS stacks add hybrid key exchanges behind negotiated suites, so apps get agility without choosing primitives manually.
comparisons.code: // configured key exchange group

comparisons.note: Go 1.23 added X25519Kyber768Draft00 as a configurable curve ID; callers opt in by name, which is not agility — it's an extra parameter.
comparisons.code: cfg := &tls.Config{CurvePreferences: []tls.CurveID{tls.X25519Kyber768Draft00}}

comparisons.note: Separate crates for classical and PQ; no unified agility envelope in std. Applications compose manually.
comparisons.code:
use aws_lc_rs::agreement::{agree_ephemeral, X25519};
// ML-KEM is a separate crate, combined by hand

decisions.bestCurrent: TLS 1.3 stacks: Modern TLS stacks add hybrid key exchanges behind negotiated suites, so apps get agility without choosing primitives manually.
decisions.recommendation: Design the agility envelope now, add PQ algorithms later. Jet should hide algorithm churn behind `seal/open` and `sign/verify`, avoiding per-call crypto menus.
decisions.comment: Why would you use a hash marker instead of just an enum for this??? Unless you have a good reason just do enum

decisions.title: Reopen wildcard imports (`use module.*`) rejected by D-MOD2?
decisions.gist: D-MOD2 rejected glob imports and wired E0612 to reject them with a clear error. The Ideas list proposes reopening `use module.*`. This is a Reopen decision: the prior rejection stands unless there is a compelling new argument.
decisions.explainer: E0612 was added deliberately: glob imports pollute the local namespace, make it impossible to know where a name came from without tooling, and break I8 (you can't tell which mechanism introduced a name). The new selective-imports card (D-SELIMPORT1) covers the actual need — bringing many names in without qualifying — without the namespace-opacity problem, by requiring the user to list the names. No new argument changes the D-MOD2 calculus. Reopening would require undoing E0612, which has a UI snapshot, and would conflict with I8.
decisions.story: I want `use math.*` so I can call `sin` without prefixing. (But: selective imports already give me `use math.{sin, cos}` with explicit names — is the glob form adding real value?)

options.name: Keep the rejection (status quo)
options.detail: E0612 stays. Selective imports (D-SELIMPORT1) cover the real need. No change. Recommended — the prior decision was well-reasoned; no new argument overturns it.

options.name: Allow glob with shadow warnings
options.detail: Lift E0612; emit a warning when a glob import shadows a local or another import. Weaker discipline than the current rejection; namespace opacity returns.
options.code:
use math.*          // warning: glob import — consider listing items
use geo.*           // warning: 'sin' shadowed by geo.sin
fn f() { sin(1.0) } // which sin?

options.name: Allow only for designated prelude modules
options.detail: A module can declare itself `prelude` and users can glob-import it. Niche mechanism; adds a concept (prelude designation) for marginal gain. Still violates I8 (two ways to introduce names).

comparisons.note: Rust allows glob imports but idiom and lints discourage them because they obscure name provenance.
comparisons.code: use module::{a, b as c};

comparisons.note: Glob imports are allowed but strongly discouraged in idiomatic Rust; clippy warns on them in most contexts.
comparisons.code: use std::collections::*; // works; not recommended

comparisons.note: `from mod import *` is allowed but considered an anti-pattern; it populates the namespace invisibly and breaks static analysis.
comparisons.code: from math import *  # works; linters flag it

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust allows glob imports but idiom and lints discourage them because they obscure name provenance.
decisions.recommendation: Keep rejecting globs. Selective imports give most convenience with stronger readability than Rust’s permissive model.

decisions.title: Add a package-scoped visibility tier (`pub(package)`) between private and `pub`?
decisions.gist: Jet currently has two visibility levels: private (default) and `pub`. In multi-package payloads, there's no way to expose something to sibling packages without making it fully public to all downstream consumers. `pub(package)` (or an equivalent spelling) fills that gap. New/Reopen — S18/D-MOD3 did not define this tier.
decisions.explainer: Multi-package payloads (owner-ratified) create the need: an internal helper shared across packages in the same payload shouldn't appear in the public API. Without this tier, authors either duplicate code or over-expose it. Blast radius: visibility rules in sema, pack.jet scope resolution, and the `pub` syntax surface. The spelling `pub(package)` mirrors Rust's `pub(crate)`; alternatives like `pub.package` or a distinct keyword (`internal`) are on the table. This sequences after D-MOD3 and the payload multi-package work. I8: this is a new semantic tier, not a second way to do an existing job — no conflict.
decisions.story: My payload has three packages: `core`, `utils`, and `cli`. `utils` has helpers that `core` and `cli` need, but I don't want them in the published API. I need one more visibility notch.

options.name: `pub(package)` spelling
options.detail: Add `pub(package)` as the package-scoped tier. Matches Rust `pub(crate)` semantics; familiar to systems programmers. Spelling is consistent with the existing `pub` keyword.

options.name: Keep private + `pub` only
options.detail: Don't add a third tier. Authors who need cross-package internals make them `pub` and rely on documentation to signal "internal". Works for small payloads; breaks down at scale.

options.name: `internal` keyword spelling
options.detail: A distinct `internal` keyword instead of `pub(package)`. Slightly more readable for beginners; one fewer parenthesized qualifier. Adds a new keyword to the surface.
options.code: internal fn hash_intern(s: str) -> u64 { … }

comparisons.note: `pub(crate)` is the idiomatic crate-scoped tier; `pub(super)` scopes to the parent module. Both are well-understood.
comparisons.code: pub(crate) fn internal_helper() {}

comparisons.note: `internal` is a keyword meaning visible within the same Gradle module — analogous to `pub(package)`.
comparisons.code: internal fun hashIntern(s: String): Long = …

decisions.title: Reopen transparent type aliases (`alias X = Y`) — declined by D-SUGAR3?
decisions.gist: S14 rejected `def` aliases and D-SUGAR3 declined transparent type aliases (a name that IS another type, fully interchangeable). The Ideas list asks to reopen. A transparent alias adds no new type-safety — `alias Meters = f64` means `Meters` and `f64` are the same type everywhere, unlike a newtype which is distinct. The reopen needs a concrete pain case that newtypes can't cover.
decisions.explainer: Newtypes (`struct Meters(f64)`) give you a distinct type with zero runtime cost, which is strictly more informative than a transparent alias. Transparent aliases are useful mainly for shortening long generic type spellings (e.g. `alias Result<T> = T ? IoError`). That's a real but narrow need. If reopened, `alias` is the preferred keyword over `def` (S14 rejected `def`). I8 check: a transparent alias for shortening a concrete generic instantiation is a different job from a newtype (distinct type); no I8 conflict for that case. But an alias for a primitive (`alias Meters = f64`) duplicates the newtype job without the safety — that case should stay declined.
decisions.story: I have `T ? ParseError ? IoError ? NetworkError` all over my code. I want `alias AppResult<T> = T ? AppError` at the top. That's not a newtype — it's a spelling shortcut for a complex type expression.

options.name: Keep declined (status quo)
options.detail: No transparent aliases. Newtypes cover the type-safety use case. Verbose generic spellings are a minor pain. D-SUGAR3 reasoning stands.
options.code:
// no alias; users repeat the full type:
fn parse(s: str) -> Token ? ParseError { … }

options.name: Add `alias X = Y` for generic type shortcuts only
options.detail: Allow `alias` only for parameterized type expressions (e.g. `alias Result<T> = T ? E`). Reject bare primitive aliases (`alias Meters = f64` → use a newtype). Narrow, concrete, no I8 conflict for the generic case.

options.name: Add `alias X = Y` fully transparent
options.detail: Allow any type alias, including primitive aliases. Simple rule; but `alias Meters = f64` gives no safety over bare `f64` and creates a second way to introduce a type name, weakening the newtype story.
options.code:
alias Meters = f64  // Meters and f64 are identical — no safety gained
alias AppResult<T> = T ? AppError

comparisons.note: Rust has fully transparent `type Alias = T`, useful for long generic signatures but not a safety boundary.
comparisons.code: type AppResult<T> = Result<T, AppError>;

comparisons.note: `type Alias = T` is fully transparent — no distinct type is created. Newtypes are `struct Foo(T)`. Both exist, but newtypes are the idiomatic safety tool.
comparisons.code:
type Meters = f64;         // transparent — no distinction
struct MetersNew(f64);     // newtype — distinct type

comparisons.note: `type` is transparent alias; `newtype` is zero-cost distinct. Haskell programmers reach for `newtype` whenever safety matters.
comparisons.code:
type Meters = Double       -- transparent
newtype MetersN = MetersN Double  -- distinct

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust has fully transparent `type Alias = T`, useful for long generic signatures but not a safety boundary.
decisions.recommendation: Allow aliases only for generic/type-expression shortcuts. Jet gets the real ergonomic win while preserving distinct types for safety.

decisions.title: Add maturity markers (`#Experimental` / `#Tested` / `#Hardened`) that propagate like effects?
decisions.gist: A maturity lattice lets library authors tag APIs with their stability level, and the compiler warns (or errors) when stable code calls experimental code without an explicit acknowledgment. New; no decision exists. The machinery would ride existing marker and effect-ceiling infrastructure.
decisions.explainer: Propagation rule: calling an `#Experimental` item taints the caller unless the caller also carries `#Experimental` or explicitly acknowledges with a suppressor (e.g. `#[allow(Experimental)]`). The lattice is `#Experimental < #Tested < #Hardened`; unmarked items default to some level (TBD — a separate question). Blast radius: sema (propagation pass), effect ceilings, doc output. Prerequisite: effect ceiling machinery needs to exist or be extended. This interacts with the effect-ceilings card. If the marker propagation model isn't yet shipped, a doc-only convention (Option B) costs nothing and covers 80% of the use-case until the machinery is ready. I1: no safety impact — this is purely about API stability signaling. I8: maturity signaling is a new job; no existing mechanism covers it.
decisions.story: I publish a library. `parse_v2` is solid; `parse_experimental` is still in flux. I tag it `#Experimental` and anyone who calls it without opting in gets a warning at their call site — not buried in a changelog.

options.name: Full propagating marker family
options.detail: Add `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as propagating markers riding existing effect machinery. Compile-time enforcement; IDE surfaces stability at call sites. Sequences after effect-ceiling machinery.

options.name: Doc-only convention now, propagation later
options.detail: Define `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as documentation-visible markers today (no compiler propagation). When effect-ceiling machinery ships, wire propagation. Low cost; covers the doc/tooling case immediately.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't decide until effect-ceiling machinery is finalized. Avoids designing the propagation model twice.
options.code: // no change; stability is communicated via doc comments only

comparisons.note: Kotlin `@RequiresOptIn` makes experimental APIs visible and can require caller opt-in.
comparisons.code: @RequiresOptIn annotation class ExperimentalApi

comparisons.note: `#[unstable]` is a compiler-enforced gate in the standard library (nightly only); third-party crates use `#[deprecated]` or doc comments. No lattice propagation.
comparisons.code:
#[unstable(feature = "new_parser", issue = "12345")]
pub fn new_parser(s: &str) -> Ast {}

comparisons.note: `@RequiresOptIn` / `@OptIn` is a propagating annotation lattice — callers must opt in or the compiler warns. Very close to what Option A proposes.

decisions.bestCurrent: Kotlin: Kotlin `@RequiresOptIn` makes experimental APIs visible and can require caller opt-in.
decisions.recommendation: Start doc-visible, propagate later. Jet should not wire a new propagation lattice until machinery is ready, but docs/IDE maturity markers can beat comment-only stability now.

decisions.title: Add named swizzle access on vector types (`.xyz`, `.wzyx`, `.xy`) — and if so, allow lvalue swizzles too?
decisions.gist: SIMD/linalg vector types exist and are ratified. Named swizzle access (`.xyz`, `.yx`, `.wzyx`) — reading or writing up to 4 lanes by name — is not yet ratified. This decides whether swizzles ship as first-class syntax or as methods, and whether write-swizzles (lvalues) are in scope.
decisions.explainer: Swizzle syntax is a subset of member access: `v.xy` would return a 2-element vector drawn from lanes x and y of `v`. It amends D-SIMD1/2. The bundle risk is separating vector-type support (done) from swizzle syntax (this card). Write-swizzles (`v.xy = .{1.0, 2.0}`) raise a second design point. Under I8, swizzle-as-method (`v.swizzle(X, Y)`) would be the only alternative that avoids new syntax — it is less ergonomic and is not how any shader/linalg library spells it. No existing ratified syntax conflicts here.
decisions.story: I'm writing a game renderer. I have a `vec4` color and I want the RGB channels as a `vec3` for a lighting calc. `col.rgb` should just work — the same as GLSL, Metal, or Zig's @shuffle. Typing `.swizzle(R, G, B)` every time is friction I don't need.
decisions.inWild:
let col: Vec4 = .{1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 1.0}
let rgb: Vec3 = col.xyz          // read swizzle
let rev: Vec4 = col.wzyx         // reverse channels
col.xy = .{0.0, 0.0}             // write swizzle (lvalue)

options.name: Blessed member swizzle (read + write)
options.detail: Generate `x/y/z/w` lane names and all N-choose-k swizzle combos as compile-time-resolved member accesses on vector lane types. Write-swizzles are lvalues. This matches shader-language and game-engine convention and needs no method call.

options.name: Blessed member swizzle (read-only)
options.detail: Same as A but write-swizzles are deferred — too complex to lower cleanly for overlapping lanes (e.g. `v.xx = ...`). Read swizzles cover 90% of the use case today.

options.name: Explicit method only
options.detail: Keep the surface minimal; expose `.x()`, `.y()` single-lane getters and a `swizzle(a, b, c, d)` method taking enum lane values. No new syntax. Verbose but I8-clean if swizzle syntax is genuinely new syntax over existing member access.
options.code:
let v: Vec3 = .{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}
let v2 = v.swizzle(Y, X)        // Vec2.{2.0, 1.0}

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Block swizzles until the semantic index and SIMD lowering paths are more stable. Ship single-lane `.x .y .z .w` getters only for now.
options.code:
let v: Vec3 = .{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}
let x = v.x                     // scalar, works today

comparisons.note: GLSL has read and write swizzles on all vector types; the four sets (xyzw, rgba, stpq) select the same lanes, aliased by convention.
Zig uses `@shuffle` as a builtin — functional but verbose; no dot-swizzle shorthand.
comparisons.code: const rgb = @shuffle(f32, col, undefined, [3]i32{0,1,2});

comparisons.note: glam generates named swizzle methods via proc-macro — `.xy()`, `.zyx()` etc. Explicit methods, not member access; write-swizzles absent.
comparisons.code:
let rgb: Vec3 = col.xyz();
let rev: Vec4 = col.wzyx();

decisions.title: Ratify a normalization contract for the content-addressed build cache?
decisions.gist: The build cache (BuildCache.rs / SHA256.rs) is partially implemented but its normalization contract — what counts as 'the same definition' for cache-key purposes — is not specified or tested. This decides whether we lock down a concrete contract now or leave it ad hoc.
decisions.explainer: Without a stated contract, two definitions that are semantically identical (whitespace change, renamed local, reordered doc comment) may or may not produce cache hits depending on implementation drift. A contract at the AST level (after parsing, before sema) is rename-sensitive by default but immune to whitespace and comment changes. Ratifying this establishes a correctness floor for all incremental build work and is a prerequisite for any cross-machine or reproducible-build guarantee. It touches BuildCache.rs, SHA256.rs, and the parser, and pairs with the content-addressed-definitions card.
decisions.story: I rename a local variable inside a function body. Nothing semantic changed. I don't want a cache miss — or worse, a stale hit — because the cache doesn't know whether that rename matters. I need to trust the cache.

options.name: Specify AST-level contract, rename-sensitive
options.detail: Hash the canonical AST (post-parse, pre-sema): strip whitespace and comments, keep all names as-is. Two definitions with different local names get different keys. Simple to implement, easy to test, conservative (avoids false hits). Document the contract and add a normalization test.

options.name: Specify AST-level contract, alpha-rename-invariant
options.detail: Before hashing, alpha-rename all locals to positional names (`_0`, `_1`, …). Two definitions differing only in local names produce the same key. More cache hits but more complex to implement and requires a stable renaming pass before sema.

options.name: Leave ad hoc in BuildCache.rs
options.detail: No ratified contract. The cache continues to work however BuildCache.rs happens to implement it. Risk: silent correctness bugs as implementation drifts; no test surface for the contract.
options.code:
// no contract — cache hits are implementation-defined
// renaming a local may or may not bust the cache

comparisons.note: Nix content addressing normalizes derivation inputs so identical builds share cache entries predictably.
comparisons.code: /nix/store/<hash>-pkg

comparisons.note: Nix derives cache keys from a normalized derivation ATerm (no whitespace variation); it is rename-sensitive at the attribute level. A clear, auditable contract is what makes Nix's reproducibility claims trustworthy.
comparisons.code:
# derivation hash = SHA256(normalised-ATerm-of-derivation)
# whitespace irrelevant; attribute names are part of the key

comparisons.note: Rust's incremental hashes the HIR with stable IDs; local renames do not bust the hash because HIR is already resolved. Jet can choose either policy but must choose one.
comparisons.code:
// rustc stable-hashes HIR bodies; local var names are irrelevant
// to the incremental fingerprint

decisions.bestCurrent: Nix: Nix content addressing normalizes derivation inputs so identical builds share cache entries predictably.
decisions.recommendation: Specify the AST-level, rename-sensitive contract. Jet should make cache identity explicit enough for agents and humans, not hidden in implementation details.

decisions.title: Build a jetdoc generator from the compiler semantic graph?
decisions.gist: Jet has doc comments (`///`, S49) and a live doctest mechanism (D-TEST4, implemented). The open question is whether to build `jet doc` — a tool that generates browsable API docs from parsed/type-resolved compiler output. Two sub-questions are entangled: (a) when does it ship relative to the sema index (D-SEMINDEX1/c96), and (b) what structured doc comment syntax does S49 need to add before generated docs are useful beyond a flat text dump? Doctests are already solved; this decision is about the API documentation generation surface only.
decisions.explainer: A semantic-graph doc generator reads the sema index (types, signatures, trait impls, doc comments) and emits HTML/Markdown API docs with tested examples. It is an E3 testing/docs ergonomics exit criterion. It depends on stable compiler seams (the `jet-sema` seam crate and the semantic index API card). Doctests close the loop: example code in `/// ` blocks is extracted and run as tests. Without this, doc quality decays because examples are untested. This card does not cover the LSP or IDE dossier views (those are D-DOSSIER1).
decisions.story: I publish a Jet library. I want `jet doc` to generate browsable API docs from my doc comments the same way `cargo doc` does — and I want any `/// ` example to fail CI if it stops compiling, not just silently rot.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) The inWild and Option A code use a pre-D-TEST4 doctest format; D-TEST4 is ratified — correct format is ```jet blocks with // => trailing comments. (2) Doctest execution (jet test --doctests) is already live via D-TEST4/c51; the open question is API doc generation only. (3) S49 says "plain text v1" — no structured doc section syntax is ratified; jetdoc built on this baseline can only emit a flat text dump. Either ratify S49 sections first or scope jetdoc explicitly to flat text. (4) Options A and C are functionally equivalent in sequencing (both gate on c96); the real decision is whether jetdoc is an E3 exit criterion.

options.name: Phase 1 AST doc now; Phase 2 sema-indexed when D-SEMINDEX1 lands (recommended)
options.detail: Phase 1 (Epoch 3, unblocked): a `jet doc` subcommand reads parsed public items and their raw `///` comments from the AST alone. Emits flat HTML per module: public signatures + doc text. No sema index required. Doctest execution (jet test --doctests) is already live via D-TEST4 — this adds browsable API surface only. Phase 2 (when D-SEMINDEX1/c96 is stable): upgrade to cross-linked, type-resolved, trait-impl-inclusive docs. Prerequisite before either phase: ratify S49 structured doc section syntax (currently "plain text v1") so Phase 1 emits structured sections instead of a raw text dump. Raise that as a follow-on ballot.
options.code:
$ jet doc
Building docs for mylib v0.1.0
  Phase 1 (AST): public symbols + raw doc comments
Wrote: docs/api/index.html
  note: type links and trait impls added in Phase 2 (when sema index lands)

$ jet test --doctests   # already live via D-TEST4
running 3 doctests
test mylib::add ... ok

options.name: Defer `jet doc` to Epoch 6 (after sema index + S49 sections)
options.detail: Do not build jetdoc until D-SEMINDEX1/c96 is stable and S49 structured sections are ratified. Avoids rebuilding Phase 1 when Phase 2 is ready. Doctests (D-TEST4) keep examples honest in the interim. Authors maintain hand-written Markdown. Viable internally but not for a public registry where doc quality is an ecosystem contract.

options.name: Hand-written docs only
options.detail: No generated docs tool. Doctests still run (D-TEST4). No browsable API surface. Keeps toolchain surface smaller. Only viable for small internal libraries; not scalable as the registry grows.
options.code:
// No jet doc. Docs are maintained manually in docs/.
// Examples compiled only when author writes a #Test block by hand.

comparisons.note: Swift DocC builds docs from typed declarations and links symbols across articles and API pages.
comparisons.code: /// Doc comment attached to a symbol

comparisons.note: rustdoc reads HIR/MIR and emits structured HTML. Doc tests (```` ``` ```` blocks in `///` comments) are compiled and run by `cargo test --doc`. This is the gold-standard baseline for jetdoc to match.
DocC compiles doc comments into a structured catalog; examples are verified at build time. Goes further than rustdoc with tutorials and interactive playgrounds.

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift DocC: Swift DocC builds docs from typed declarations and links symbols across articles and API pages.
decisions.recommendation: Phase 1 AST-level `jet doc` now (unblocked); Phase 2 sema-indexed upgrade when D-SEMINDEX1/c96 lands (Option A). Prerequisite: ratify S49 structured doc section syntax before either phase ships.

decisions.title: Build a dossier / outline view that stitches scattered type members across files?
decisions.gist: Jet allows methods and impls of a type to live in multiple files. Today there is no editor view that collects all of a type's members into one outline. This decides whether to build that view, and whether to gate it on a stable semantic index API.
decisions.explainer: A dossier view would use the LSP and semantic index to show every method, field, and impl of a type in a single outline panel, regardless of which files they live in. It supports the Blueprint north-star (memory): type-directed authoring where you see the full shape of a type without hunting across files. It depends on the stable semantic-index API card — building it before that API is locked risks throwing the work away. It is purely tooling (no language surface changes) and does not block any compiler invariants, but it affects the LSP sub-system. D-BREADCRUMB1 is the companion card for in-editor phantom stubs.
decisions.story: I'm working on a large type that has impls spread across five files — rendering, serialization, physics. I want one panel that shows me everything this type can do, so I can navigate without grep. Like an Unreal Blueprint node, but for my entire type.

options.name: Build dossier as LSP code-lens / outline, gated on semantic index
options.detail: Add a dossier outline command to the LSP server, powered by the semantic index once its API is stable. The editor extension surfaces it as a sidebar panel or `Go to type outline` command. Gate: semantic-index API must be ratified and stable first.

options.name: Defer until semantic index API is stable
options.detail: Explicitly defer — mark the card as blocked on semantic-index API ratification. Then build it as option A describes. Avoids a rebuild if the index API changes significantly, but delays the Blueprint north-star ergonomic win.
options.code:
// no dossier view today
// unblock when D-SEMIDX1 is ratified

options.name: Skip (use grep / LSP workspace symbols)
options.detail: Don't build a dossier view. Authors use the standard LSP workspace-symbols search or text grep to find scattered members. Keeps LSP surface smaller but leaves the Blueprint north-star incomplete.
options.code:
// status quo: Ctrl+T → workspace symbol search
// results: all symbols matching query across all files

comparisons.note: Smalltalk browsers organize behavior by class/protocol rather than file, making scattered methods coherent.
comparisons.code: Class browser: Point -> methods

comparisons.note: The 'Structure' panel shows all members of the current class. It does not stitch across files (separate impls show separately). Jet's dossier would go further.
comparisons.code:
// Structure panel: shows fields + methods of current file's class
// multi-file impls are NOT stitched — you see one file at a time

comparisons.note: Blueprint shows every event, function, and variable on a class as typed pins in one graph. The dossier is the textual analog: one place to see the full type contract.
comparisons.code:
// Blueprint node: all inputs/outputs visible at once
// no hunting across multiple graph views for the same actor

decisions.bestCurrent: Smalltalk: Smalltalk browsers organize behavior by class/protocol rather than file, making scattered methods coherent.
decisions.recommendation: Defer until the semantic index is stable. Jet should match Smalltalk’s navigability, but only once cross-file member identity is complete.

decisions.title: Show phantom breadcrumb hints for methods defined away from the type body?
decisions.gist: When a type has methods defined in other files, the type's own source file shows nothing about them. Breadcrumb hints would inject phantom (non-editable) stubs near the type body in the editor, listing methods defined elsewhere. This is a companion to the dossier view.
decisions.explainer: Breadcrumb hints are LSP inlay hints or code-lens annotations injected at the type declaration site, listing methods defined in other files with clickable jump-to-definition links. They add no language semantics — purely a tooling overlay. They depend on the same stable semantic index API as D-DOSSIER1. Building both on the same index pass is efficient; building either before the index API is locked risks rework. Under I8, this does not add a new language mechanism — it is an editor affordance only.
decisions.story: I'm reading `model.jet` and I see `struct Player`. I know there are rendering and physics methods somewhere, but the struct body is silent. I want ghost text just below the struct telling me '+ 4 methods in render.jet, physics.jet' with jump links — so I don't have to grep.

options.name: LSP inlay / code-lens phantom stubs, gated on semantic index
options.detail: Emit LSP inlay hints or code-lens items at the type declaration listing away-methods. Clickable → jump to definition. Gate: same semantic-index API stability requirement as D-DOSSIER1. Build both on the same pass.

options.name: Defer (same gate as dossier view)
options.detail: Defer explicitly — blocked on semantic-index API ratification. Once that unblocks D-DOSSIER1, breadcrumb hints can ship in the same pass. Avoids piecemeal work and rework risk.
options.code:
// no phantom stubs today
// unblock with D-DOSSIER1 when semantic index is stable

options.name: Skip
options.detail: Don't add phantom stubs. The dossier view (D-DOSSIER1) already gives a type outline on demand; inline hints are redundant if the panel exists. Keeps LSP surface smaller.
options.code:
// status quo: type body shows only its own members
// use dossier panel or workspace search for away-methods

comparisons.note: JetBrains IDEs expose declarations away from the current file through structure views, inlays, and navigation markers.
comparisons.code: // IDE inlay: implements Foo.bar

comparisons.note: C# Dev Kit shows 'X references' code-lens above methods and types. It does not show away-methods at the declaration site — closer to a reference count than a stub listing.
comparisons.code:
// 5 references  ← code-lens above the class
class Player { ... }

comparisons.note: Rust-analyzer emits inlay hints (parameter names, return types) but no phantom stubs for trait impls defined elsewhere. Jet breadcrumbs would go further for the multi-file impl case.
comparisons.code:
// inlay hints: parameter names and types inline
// no phantom stubs for impl blocks in other files

decisions.bestCurrent: JetBrains IDEs: JetBrains IDEs expose declarations away from the current file through structure views, inlays, and navigation markers.
decisions.recommendation: Defer with dossier work. Phantom stubs need the same semantic identity graph, so they should not precede the index.

decisions.title: Add a first-class `workspace.jet` workspace manifest for multi-package repos, or reuse `pack.jet payload:`?
decisions.gist: Multi-package repos need a way to declare a set of member packages. `pack.jet payload:` already handles multi-package core sources. This decides whether to introduce a separate `workspace.jet` root manifest or rely on the existing `payload:` mechanism.
decisions.explainer: The `payload:` field in `pack.jet` lets a single package declare multiple member packages (memory: payload-multi-package-core-source). A `workspace.jet` would be a new top-level file with no associated package, purely grouping independent packages for a shared build/tooling context (shared lock file, cross-member `pub(package)` visibility, unified `jet build`). The key question is whether `payload:` semantics already cover the monorepo case or whether they differ enough to justify a new file type. Under I8, two files solving the same grouping job is a strike unless they cover genuinely different semantic territory. This was a live owner decision in Tower c156.
decisions.story: I have a repo with four separate Jet packages — a compiler, a CLI, a stdlib, and a test runner. I want `jet build` at the repo root to build all of them, with a single lock file and cross-package visibility. I don't want one of them to be the 'master' package that owns the others.
decisions.inWild:
# workspace.jet (proposed)
[workspace]
members = [
    "crates/compiler",
    "crates/cli",
    "crates/stdlib",
    "crates/test-runner",
]

# vs. pack.jet payload: (existing)
[payload]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

options.name: Add `workspace.jet` (separate workspace manifest)
options.detail: A new top-level `workspace.jet` file with no owning package — purely a grouping manifest. Members are independent packages each with their own `pack.jet`. Supports a shared lock file, `pub(package)`, and unified `jet` commands. Clearest model for repos where no single package is 'the root'.
options.code:
# workspace.jet
[workspace]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

$ jet build           # builds all members
$ jet test --all      # tests all members

options.name: Reuse `pack.jet payload:` (no new file)
options.detail: The root `pack.jet` with a `payload:` section already declares member packages. Extend its semantics: if `payload:` is present with no `[package]` section, it acts as a pure workspace root. No new file type; I8-clean if `payload:` already covers this exactly.
options.code:
# pack.jet (workspace root, no [package] section)
[payload]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

$ jet build           # builds all payload members

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't ratify a workspace surface yet. Multi-package builds work today by running `jet build` in each package directory. Defer until the lock-file and `pub(package)` designs are settled, so the workspace contract is informed by what it actually needs to coordinate.
options.code:
# no workspace manifest; run per-package:
$ jet build -C crates/compiler
$ jet build -C crates/cli

comparisons.note: Cargo uses a root `Cargo.toml` with `[workspace]` members list. The root may or may not also declare a `[package]`. Members share a `Cargo.lock` and `target/`.
comparisons.code:
[workspace]
members = ["crates/*"]
resolver = "2"

comparisons.note: npm uses a root `package.json` with a `workspaces` array. The root is itself a package. Closer to Jet's `pack.jet payload:` model than to a separate file.
comparisons.code:
// package.json
{ "workspaces": ["packages/*"] }

decisions.comment: Reconciled 2026-06-27: canonical D-WORKSPACE1 in docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md is B — fully computable workspace.jet. This Tower card's option labels predate the owner-modified ratification; follow D-WORKSPACE1/D-WORKSPACE2 in syntax-decisions.md.

decisions.title: Add generic modules (ML-functor-style module parameterized by a type or value)?
decisions.gist: Jet has generic types and functions. Generic modules — a module parameterized by a type or value at the module level, instantiated to produce a new module — do not exist. This decides whether to add them or keep the surface at generic types and functions only.
decisions.explainer: ML-style functors let you write `module Map(K: Ord)` and instantiate it as `module IntMap = Map(Int)`. The result is a new module with all members specialized to `K = Int`. In Jet, generic types already handle the common case (`Map[K: Ord, V]`); generic modules go further by allowing module-level abstraction (sharing multiple related types, hiding implementation modules, enforcing interface contracts at the module boundary). Under I8, if generic types already cover the use case, a second mechanism is a strike. The complexity is high: module instantiation affects name resolution, the module graph, and comptime. There is no ratified syntax precedent in Jet for module-level generics.
decisions.story: I'm building a pluggable hash-map where the key comparison strategy is a module (not just a function). I want `module HashMap(K: KeyModule)` where `KeyModule` supplies `hash`, `eq`, and an associated `Error` type — none of which are cleanly expressible as a single generic type parameter.

options.name: Add generic modules (ML-functor style)
options.detail: Ratify module-level parameterization. A module can declare type/value parameters; instantiation produces a new named module. Requires new syntax, new name-resolution rules, and comptime integration. Only justified if a concrete use case cannot be served by generic types alone.

options.name: Keep generic types and functions only (status quo)
options.detail: The existing `Type[T: Trait]` and `fn foo[T: Trait]()` cover the overwhelming majority of parameterization needs. Module-level generics add complexity for a narrow use case. Reject until a concrete case proves generic types are insufficient. I8-clean.

options.name: Defer pending concrete use case
options.detail: Don't reject outright — park the card until a real Jet codebase hits the wall with generic types and functions and needs functor-level abstraction. Then revisit with a concrete motivating example.
options.code:
// deferred: no syntax or implementation
// reopen when a concrete stdlib or user case requires it

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are the canonical ML-functor. `module Map.Make(Ord)` produces a map module specialized to `Ord.t`. Widely used but notoriously hard to read for newcomers.
comparisons.code:
module IntMap = Map.Make(Int)
let m = IntMap.add 1 "one" IntMap.empty

comparisons.note: Rust has no module generics — generic types and traits cover the use case. This is the status-quo model Jet already follows; it has proven sufficient for a production systems language.
comparisons.code:
// No generic modules; use generic structs + traits:
struct HashMap<K: Hash + Eq, V> { ... }

decisions.title: What exact syntax distinguishes generic-module type parameters, value parameters, and instantiation?
decisions.gist: Before choosing a spelling: resolve the conflict with D-GENMOD1's floor example (paren type params) and D-LINALG1's blessed `<N>` value-in-angles. The current option set contains no choice that is consistent with both prior decisions simultaneously. A new option (annotation-kind in `<...>`, no extra keyword) resolves both. The "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling may also close Options A–C entirely; confirm its scope before proceeding.
decisions.explainer: Owner instruction integrated: Jet generics use `<T>`, so generic modules must not invent `[]` for type parameters. Adversarial pass: mixing type and value parameters can become C++-template soup or force users to guess whether an argument is a type or value. Patch: keep type parameters in `<...>`, keep compile-time value parameters in `(...)`, and require instantiation to mirror declaration. If that still feels too large for E3, choose the Epoch 6 defer option and keep ordinary generic structs/functions as the only generic surface for now.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a fixed-size LRU cache package. The key type controls hashing/equality, while the capacity is a compile-time value. She wants one generic module that exports `Cache`, `put`, and `get`, then instantiates `StringCache32` once for the rest of the package.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Address GENMOD2; integrate the instruction that Jet generics use `<T>`, provide better options, and include an option to defer to Epoch 6.
Agent answer: Corrected. The previous `[]` type-parameter option was wrong for Jet because `[]` already reads as list/indexing while `<T>` is the ratified generic form. Updated options now center `<T>` for type parameters, separate compile-time value parameters with `(...)`, and add an Epoch 6 defer option.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIOR DECISION CONFLICTS (must resolve before any option is adopted): D-GENMOD1's ratified code example uses `module Sorted(T: Ord)` — type param in parens; Option A contradicts this. D-LINALG1 blessed Vec<N> (value-in-<...>) as the substrate spelling; Option A puts values in (...), directly contradicting. The comptime section of syntax-decisions.md says "Rejected: const generics in v1" — module value parameters are const generics and this rejection may apply. PARSER HAZARD (Option A): `Lru<String>(32)` is syntactically identical to D-SERDE6 turbofish `fn<T>(arg)`; parser cannot resolve without name-resolution, violating parse-before-sema. VOCABULARY HAZARD (Option B): `const` is a teaching-error-only keyword (S14); using it inside `<...>` is the first real use. MISSING OPTION E: unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` with annotation-kind as distinguisher — consistent with D-LINALG1, avoids all vocabulary collisions.

options.name: Unified `<...>`: annotation kind distinguishes type vs value params (recommended)
options.detail: Both type and value parameters live in `<...>`. A parameter whose annotation is a bound/trait (`K: Hash`) is a type parameter; one whose annotation is a value type (`capacity: Int`) is a value parameter — no extra keyword, no dual-bracket syntax. Instantiation mirrors declaration: `Lru<String, 32>`. Consistent with D-LINALG1's `Vec<N>` substrate (value-in-angles already blessed). Supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example which used parens — that was explicitly a placeholder "until GENMOD2 decides." Parser: distinguishes a type expression (capital-cased, D-CASING1) from a value expression at instantiation sites in `<...>` — mostly mechanical at the lexer level.

options.name: Defer generic modules to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not add module-level type/value parameters now. Ordinary generic structs and functions (`fn sort<T: Ord>`, `struct Vec<T>`) already cover most use cases. Defer if the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling in the comptime section applies to module value parameters, or if the D-LINALG1 `Vec<N>` value-parameter surface needs a unified ruling before any single site commits.

options.name: Ordinary generic types/fns only — no module-level parameters
options.detail: Decline generic modules entirely. Priya's LRU cache is a generic struct with a capacity field; the type-level instantiation story is solved by generic types already. Module-level parameters are a second mechanism for the same parametrization job (I8 risk). Only reconsider if a concrete use case cannot be expressed with generic types.

comparisons.note: Rust uses `<T>` for type parameters and also has const generics in `<...>`. Good precedent for Option B, but Jet should avoid forcing values into type syntax unless needed.
comparisons.code: struct Ring<T, const N: usize> { ... }

comparisons.note: C++ templates mix type and value parameters in angle brackets. Powerful, but visually dense and a known complexity sink.
comparisons.code: template<typename K, int N> struct Lru { ... };

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are module-level generics, but parameters are module-shaped. Powerful, less beginner-direct than Jet’s desired package surface.
comparisons.code: module IntMap = Map.Make(Int)

comparisons.note: Zig uses comptime parameters in function-like declarations; clear for values, but Jet already has `<T>` for type generics.
comparisons.code: fn Lru(comptime K: type, comptime capacity: usize) type { ... }

decisions.recommendation: Unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` — annotation kind distinguishes type vs value parameters in `<...>` (Option A). Consistent with D-LINALG1's Vec<N>; supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example. If the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling applies, choose Option B (defer).

decisions.title: Add variadic function parameters and spread syntax (`...xs` call spread, `[...a, ...b]` list spread)?
decisions.gist: Jet has no variadic function parameters and no spread syntax. D-FP6 deferred list spread. This decides whether to add all three (variadic params, call spread, list spread) under a single sigil, and which sigil to use — aware that fan-out `f.[a,b,c]` (S75) is already ratified.
decisions.explainer: Three related but separable features: (1) variadic params (`fn log(msgs: ...String)`), (2) call spread (`log(...msgs)`), and (3) list spread (`[...a, ...b]`). They share a surface sigil. The tension: fan-out `f.[a,b,c]` (S75) already provides one form of multi-argument application, and list spread overlaps conceptually with concatenation. Under I8, spreading must not duplicate what fan-out already does. The spread sigil (`...`) is the JavaScript/TypeScript convention; Jet has no precedent for it. A new sigil needs owner ratification. Variadics also affect codegen (Rust does not have variadics; lowering requires a slice or tuple approach).
decisions.story: I'm writing a logging function that takes any number of strings. I want `log("user:", name, "age:", age)` without building an array first. And when I have a list `parts` already, I want `log(...parts)` to expand it at the call site — not write a different function.

options.name: Add all three under `...` sigil
options.detail: Ratify `...` as the spread/rest sigil. Variadic params use `name: ...T` (rest position, last param only). Call spread uses `f(...xs)`. List spread uses `[...a, ...b]`. Lowers variadic params to a slice `[T]` in codegen. Must verify no overlap with fan-out S75.
options.code:
fn sum(ns: ...Int) -> Int { ns.fold(0, fn(a,b){a+b}) }
let xs = [1, 2, 3]
sum(...xs)                     // 6
let ys = [...xs, 4, 5]         // [1,2,3,4,5]

options.name: List spread only (re-open D-FP6)
options.detail: Ratify `[...a, ...b]` list spread only. Variadic params and call spread are deferred. Covers the most common non-function use case without touching function signatures or the call protocol.
options.code:
let a = [1, 2]
let b = [3, 4]
let c = [...a, ...b]           // [1,2,3,4]
// variadic fn params: still not available

options.name: Variadic params only (no spread sigil yet)
options.detail: Add variadic params (`name: ...T`) as a language feature; do not ratify a spread sigil. Call sites pass individual args or an explicit slice. Avoids ratifying `...` before deciding its full scope.

options.name: Keep deferred (status quo)
options.detail: Maintain the D-FP6 deferral. Fan-out `f.[a,b,c]` covers multi-application; explicit list construction covers concatenation. Add variadics only when a stdlib function genuinely needs them and there is no I8-clean alternative.

comparisons.note: TypeScript has rest params (`...args: string[]`) and spread in calls and arrays. The `...` sigil is overloaded across all three contexts; it is the most common model in modern languages.
Python uses `*args` for variadic params and `*seq` for call/list spread. Separate sigils (`*` vs `**`) for positional vs keyword. Functional but two-sigil complexity.
comparisons.code:
def log(*msgs): print(*msgs)
parts = ['a','b']
log(*parts)
all_ = [*parts, 'c']

decisions.title: Define a versioned public semantic-index query API?
decisions.gist: The compiler already builds a rich symbol database internally (Source/LSP/SymbolDB.rs: symbols, types, references, call graph). Right now that data is internal-only — no external tool can query it without forking compiler internals. This decision is whether to promote a stable, versioned subset of that data into a public API that tools (IDE plugins, impact analyzers, dossier, ask-your-codebase) can depend on.
decisions.explainer: A public semantic-index API is listed as an Epoch 4 exit criterion. It is the prerequisite for three other queued ideas — impact-analyzer (D-IMPACT1), codemods (D-CODEMOD1), and ask-your-codebase — all of which need reliable, versioned access to compiler facts. The API would live on top of the seam crates (compiler-workspace-seams: jet-sema, jet-foundation) and be versioned independently of the compiler internals. It does not change language semantics or surface syntax, so I1/I8 are not in play. Sequencing risk: if the internal SymbolDB layout changes significantly before the API is frozen, the versioning story becomes harder; starting the freeze now reduces that drift.
decisions.story: I'm writing a refactor tool. I need to know every call site of a function, the type of each argument, and which tests exercise it — without running the compiler myself. I want to query that from a stable interface that won't break when the compiler's internals change.

options.name: Versioned public API over seam crates
options.detail: Expose a stable, versioned query surface (symbols, types, references, call graph) as a public crate built on jet-sema/jet-foundation. Tools depend on the API version, not compiler internals. This is the E4 exit criterion and unlocks impact analysis, codemods, and dossier.

options.name: Keep internal-only
options.detail: No public API. External tools must parse source themselves or shell out to the LSP. Simpler for the compiler team; blocks all downstream tooling ideas indefinitely.
options.code:
// current state: tools use LSP textDocument/references
// (network protocol, not a typed query API, no type info)

options.name: Defer past E4
options.detail: Accept the E4 exit criterion slip. Useful if the internal SymbolDB is still in heavy flux and freezing it now would be costly. Leaves downstream cards blocked.
options.code:
// no change; D-IMPACT1, D-CODEMOD1, ask-your-codebase
// all remain blocked

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer exposes a public `ide` crate with typed queries (find_all_refs, go_to_def, call_hierarchy). Third-party tools depend on it. It is versioned separately from the compiler.
ts-morph wraps the TypeScript compiler API into a stable typed query surface. Tools use it for refactoring and analysis without touching compiler internals.
comparisons.code:
const refs = sourceFile.getReferencedSymbols();
refs.forEach(r => console.log(r.getDefinition().getFilePath()));

decisions.title: Build an impact / blast-radius analyzer on top of the semantic-index API?
decisions.gist: When you change a function signature, add a field, or rename a type, it is not obvious how many things break downstream. An impact analyzer reports the full blast radius of a proposed change — callers, dependent types, and affected tests — before you commit it. No such tool exists for Jet today. This decision is whether to build one, and whether to sequence it after D-SEMINDEX1.
decisions.explainer: This card has a hard prerequisite: the semantic-index query API (D-SEMINDEX1). Without a stable, typed query surface, the analyzer would have to duplicate compiler internals or use fragile text heuristics. If D-SEMINDEX1 is approved, this card can proceed immediately after. The tool is purely additive — it reads the index and reports; it does not change language semantics (I1/I8 not in play). Blast-radius reporting is also an input to the codemod system (D-CODEMOD1): you want to know the impact before you replay a codemod.
decisions.story: Before I rename `payments::charge` to `payments::bill`, I want to see exactly how many files change, which tests are affected, and whether any public API is broken — without actually making the change yet.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet impact payments::charge --rename payments::bill
Blast radius: 12 call sites across 4 files
  src/billing.jet:44  src/invoice.jet:19  ...
Affected tests: 3 (#Unit, #Integration)
Public API: yes — exported symbol

options.name: Build on semantic-index API, sequence after D-SEMINDEX1
options.detail: Implement `jet impact` as a CLI tool (and LSP hover/codelens) that queries the semantic index for callers, dependents, and test coverage. Sequence it after D-SEMINDEX1 is shipped. Clean separation: query layer does the work, this tool just renders it.
options.code:
$ jet impact auth::Session --change remove-field:token
Blast radius:
  8 read sites  (src/auth.jet, src/session.jet, ...)
  2 write sites (src/login.jet:71, src/refresh.jet:22)
  Tests affected: 5
  Breaking public API: no

options.name: Standalone, no semantic-index dependency
options.detail: Build the analyzer against compiler internals directly, not a public API. Faster to start but tightly coupled; breaks whenever internals change. Violates the intended seam-crate architecture.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Wait until more of the tooling ecosystem is defined. Low cost now; leaves developers without blast-radius visibility indefinitely.

// or rely on compile errors after the change

decisions.title: Model refactors as named, shippable, reversible codemod objects?
decisions.gist: Today the LSP supports one-shot fixes and renames, but there is no way to package a refactor as a named, versionable object that can be shipped to a team, replayed on a different branch, or undone. This decision is whether to introduce a codemod object model — named transformations backed by the semantic index — as a first-class Jet tooling concept.
decisions.explainer: This card depends on the semantic-index API (D-SEMINDEX1) for reliable symbol resolution and on the impact analyzer (D-IMPACT1) for pre-flight blast-radius checks. It is also complementary to content-addressed definitions (if ratified): if definitions are content-addressed, a codemod can reference the pre- and post-image by hash rather than by name, making reversal exact. The codemod object model is pure tooling — no language syntax change, no I1/I8 impact. The risk is over-engineering: if one-shot LSP fixes cover 90% of real refactor needs, a full object model may be premature.
decisions.story: My team is upgrading an API across 30 files. I want to define the rename once, preview it, commit the codemod as a named artifact so others can replay it on their branches, and undo it cleanly if the API changes again.

options.name: Named codemod objects on top of semantic-index + replay log
options.detail: Define a `.codemod.jet` format: a named transformation (rename, signature change, pattern substitution) backed by semantic-index resolution. Include a replay log so it can be applied on a different branch and undone cleanly. Sequence after D-SEMINDEX1 and D-IMPACT1.
options.code:
$ jet codemod apply rename-charge.codemod.jet
Applying RenameCharge:
  modified: src/billing.jet (3 sites)
  modified: src/invoice.jet (1 site)
Log written: .jet/codemods/rename-charge.log
$ jet codemod undo rename-charge.codemod.jet
Reverted 4 sites

options.name: Keep ad-hoc LSP fixes only
options.detail: One-shot rename/fix via the LSP; no named objects, no replay, no undo log. Sufficient for small codebases; breaks down when a refactor spans branches or needs to be shared across a team.
options.code:
// LSP: workspace/applyEdit for a rename
// No replay, no undo, no sharing

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Wait until D-SEMINDEX1 and D-IMPACT1 are proven in practice before designing the codemod model. Lower risk of over-engineering; delays the team-sharing use case.
options.code:
// no change; team shares refactor scripts
// manually (fragile, no semantic resolution)

comparisons.note: Rustfix applies machine-readable compiler suggestions; most codemods are text/AST scripts without semantic replay.
comparisons.code: cargo fix --edition

comparisons.note: jscodeshift lets you write a transform function, apply it to many files, and share it as an npm package. No built-in undo or semantic resolution — it works on AST, not types.
`cargo fix` applies machine-applicable compiler suggestions automatically. Not user-authored, not named, not reversible — but shows the pattern of compiler-guided rewrites.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo fix --allow-dirty
Fixing src/main.rs (2 fixes applied)

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rustfix applies machine-readable compiler suggestions; most codemods are text/AST scripts without semantic replay.
decisions.recommendation: Model codemods as named semantic refactors. Jet can beat rustfix by making refactors shippable, reversible, and validated against the index.

decisions.title: Should coroutines stay an internal runtime substrate or become a user-facing primitive?
decisions.gist: Resolve two separate questions the current framing conflates: (1) Should coroutine-grade control (pause/resume/trace/scheduler policy) be exposed through task handles, or deferred? (2) Should lazy sequences (generators, resumable parsers, yield-based state machines) get their own yield fn primitive? This ballot answers (1); question (2) requires a separate D-GENERATOR1 card regardless of which option is chosen here.
decisions.explainer: Owner questions answered: D-COROUTINE1 sits under the structured-concurrency stack. The coherent model is ordinary code -> `task`/channels -> nursery/taskgroup owns lifetime -> `race`/`all`/`any`/select are scoped combinators -> deadlines/cancellation flow through context -> the M:N scheduler parks tasks on I/O/timers. A gives direct source-level suspend/resume; B gives expert power through the canonical task object. Adversarial pass: B can look like less control. Patch: B explicitly includes task handles, scheduler contexts, pause/resume/cancel, priority/pinning where supported, tracing, replay hooks, and debugger visibility. What B withholds is arbitrary resumable frames outside task scope.
decisions.story: I am writing a server. I want blocking-looking socket reads to scale to 100k idle connections, but I do not want every helper in my program to become async-colored or every beginner to learn a coroutine primitive.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: What is the relationship to all the other concurrency decisions/plans?
Agent answer: Reconciled in tools/Tower/docs/plans/epoch-3/concurrency-vision.md. The coherent model: ordinary Jet code → task{}/channels → nursery scopes own task lifetime → all/race/any are nursery combinators → deadlines/cancellation flow through nursery context → M:N scheduler parks tasks on I/O/timers. D-COROUTINE1 decides whether coroutines stay internal substrate (rec B); D-NURSERY1 chooses the structured-concurrency scope; D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 fold into that scope.

Owner Q: Is there anything that cannot be accomplished with option B that could be accomplished with option A?
Agent answer: A gives direct user-written suspend/resume and generator syntax. B gives the same runtime power through task handles (pause/resume/cancel/trace/scheduler policy). What B cannot do: let arbitrary application code become its own resumable frame independent of task scope. If the job is concurrency, task/nursery/channel/select is the one path; if the job is generators/iterators, raise a separate generator card.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): GAP — lazy evaluation: B does not answer the computation dimension (lazy sequences, resumable parsers). Option E (D-GENERATOR1) is required to close this gap. GAP — pause/deadline cohesion: h.pause() interaction with D-DEADLINE1=A propagation is unspecified — if a deadline fires while a task is paused, the behavior must be defined. FRAMING: B withholds free-floating coroutine objects and yield-in-function, not coroutine control power. NEW CARD REQUIRED: D-GENERATOR1 — lazy sequences/yield functions, caller-driven, no scheduler.

options.name: Task handles provide coroutine-grade control; raise D-GENERATOR1 for lazy sequences (recommended)
options.detail: The M:N scheduler uses continuations internally. Experts access suspension control through scoped task handles: cancel, pause, resume, priority/fidelity, trace, deadline inspection, and deterministic replay hooks. What this withholds: a second user-level coroutine object for arbitrary async work outside task scope (redundant with tasks for concurrency). What this does NOT address: the lazy-sequence / generator use case (caller-driven, single-threaded step-computation, no scheduler). Raise D-GENERATOR1 as a new ballot immediately: `yield fn` that turns a function into a lazy `Iter<T>`, no scheduler involvement, orthogonal to task concurrency.

options.name: User-facing coroutine/generator primitive
options.detail: Adds a suspend/resume surface usable as a scheduler-managed async primitive (competes with tasks — overlaps task/channel/nursery, reintroduces D-ASYNCRT1's rejected function-coloring problem) or as a generator for lazy sequences (a legitimate gap). These two modes must be separated. The concurrency dimension is clearly wrong given D-ASYNCRT1=A; the computation dimension belongs in D-GENERATOR1.

options.name: Defer coroutine substrate choices to Epoch 6
options.detail: Ship only task/channel/taskgroup semantics with cancel and wait on handles. No expert scheduling controls (pause, resume, priority, trace, replay) until Epoch 6. Correct only if the team wants to discover real expert-control needs from production programs before designing the API.

comparisons.note: Python exposes generators and async coroutines as distinct concepts; the overlap is a known source of confusion. Jet should avoid that split in the beginner surface.

def gen(): yield x

decisions.bestCurrent: Go hides scheduler suspension behind blocking-looking code; Kotlin shows coroutine substrate power but at the cost of visible suspend coloring.
decisions.recommendation: Task handles expose coroutine-grade control; coroutine substrate stays internal (Option A). Raise D-GENERATOR1 as a new ballot immediately — lazy sequences are a separate, orthogonal problem not answered here.
