decisions.title: Should Jet express resource/time budgets as types and statically warn when a called function exceeds them — and if so, in what form?
decisions.gist: A render-frame loop wants a 16ms CPU budget that the compiler can enforce. But sound static timing/cost inference (WCET) is research-grade and undecidable in general — you cannot prove a wall-clock bound from source. The honest split: decline it as a type, ship a foundational #Budget that is really an effect/capability ceiling (forbid known-expensive effects in a hot region), or commit to full RAML-style cost inference as a post-Epoch research track.
decisions.explainer: Real timing budgets are a runtime property of a specific machine, inputs, and cache state; proving a 16ms bound at compile time is the worst-case-execution-time (WCET) problem, which is undecidable in general and, where tractable, requires whole-program loop-bound annotations and a hardware cost model (Ada/SPARK + aiT, RAML's amortized analysis). None of that is an Epoch-3 feature, and none of it composes with I8 without inventing a parallel mechanism. The pragmatic insight: most frame-budget blowups in practice come from doing forbidden *kinds* of work in a hot path — heap allocation, IO, syscalls, unbounded loops. Jet already has the exact machinery to forbid effect categories in a region (#(…) bounds, #Caps(…) ceilings, E0740/E0741). A #Budget region is therefore not a timing proof at all — it is an effect ceiling with a cost-oriented name that bans Alloc/Io/Net and flags unbounded loops, giving real, sound guarantees (no allocation in the render path) without claiming a millisecond it cannot honor. Full cost inference (option C) stays an honest research item; the runtime deadline path (option A's pointer to D-DEADLINE1) is the sanctioned way to get actual wall-clock enforcement today.
decisions.story: I'm writing render_frame for a 60fps game and I keep blowing my 16ms budget because some helper deep in the call graph quietly allocates and hits the filesystem to lazy-load a texture. I want the compiler to tell me — at the call site, before I ship — that this hot path is doing something it must never do, instead of finding it in a profiler at 11fps.

options.name: Decline budgets-as-types — sanction the runtime path (D-DEADLINE1)
options.detail: Do not add any budget type or marker. A wall-clock budget is a runtime fact, so enforce it at runtime: the existing latency/deadline-propagation card (D-DEADLINE1) carries a deadline on #Context and cancels work past it, and ordinary profiling catches regressions. The compiler makes no timing claim it cannot prove. Honest about undecidability; smallest surface; risks leaving the 'no alloc in the hot path' guarantee that game/audio devs actually want unserved.

options.name: Foundational #Budget marker — a cost-oriented effect ceiling (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship #Budget(name) as a region/function marker that is a thin policy layer over the existing effect ceiling (#Caps / #(…)). A budget profile names forbidden effects (default: Alloc, Io, Net, Fs) and requires every loop in the region to have a statically known bound. Reuses E0741's machinery; new diagnostics E0746 (forbidden effect in budget) and E0747 (unbounded loop in budget). It is NOT a timing proof — it proves the region does no expensive *kind* of work and has no unbounded iteration, which is the sound, decidable core devs can rely on. Composes with effect ceilings under I8 (one mechanism: effect bounds), not a parallel system. Names the limit honestly: a budget is a no-alloc/no-IO/bounded-loop contract, not 16ms.

options.name: Full static cost-bound inference (RAML-style, post-Epoch research)
options.detail: Commit to real comptime cost inference: a #Budget(16ms) (or abstract cost units) that the compiler discharges by inferring an amortized worst-case cost bound for each function and proving the called set fits. This is automatic amortized resource analysis (RAML) plus a hardware/instruction cost model — research-grade, requires loop-bound annotations or a termination/ranking analysis, an LP solver in comptime, and is undecidable in general (only sound on an annotated, restricted fragment). Highest value if it lands, but it cannot ship in Epoch 3, would pull a solver into the I6-clean compiler, and risks promising millisecond bounds the model can't honor across machines. Keep as a flagged research track that option B's effect ceiling forward-composes into.

comparisons.note: Real-time systems express priorities/deadlines; full static cost inference is rare and niche.
comparisons.code: pragma Priority(System.Priority'Last);

comparisons.note: The hard-real-time world separates the two halves Jet must not conflate: the *language* (Ravenscar profile) statically forbids dynamic constructs in critical tasks — no unbounded allocation, no unbounded loops, restricted tasking — which is exactly option B's effect/capability ceiling. The actual *16ms timing proof* is done by a separate external WCET tool (aiT) over the binary with a CPU model, never by the type system. This is the prior-art case for declining timing-as-a-type while shipping the restriction profile.
comparisons.code:
-- Ravenscar restricts the language for the hot path (≈ option B):
pragma Profile (Ravenscar);   -- no dynamic alloc, bounded tasking
-- The 16ms bound is proven OUTSIDE the type system, by aiT WCET analysis on the binary.

comparisons.note: Two contrasting points. EVM proves cost only by *running* with a runtime gas counter that aborts when exhausted — dynamic, not static — mirroring option A's runtime-deadline path; even there the static bound is undecidable so it's metered live. Koka shows the decidable, sound thing you CAN infer: it infers *effect rows* (which effects a function has), not costs — confirming that effect membership is tractable and composable while cost magnitude is not. Jet's #Budget(B) leans on the Koka-style effect inference it already has, and leaves the EVM-style magnitude question to runtime.

decisions.bestCurrent: RTSJ / Ada: Real-time systems express priorities/deadlines; full static cost inference is rare and niche.
decisions.recommendation: Use a foundational `#Budget` marker, not full cost inference. Jet can connect budgets to effects/deadlines now and leave exact proofs to research.

decisions.title: Should Jet support reversible/constraint-solved values — write `width = parent.width - padding*2` and let the compiler solve for `padding` given a target `width` — and if so, as a general language feature or only as a scoped UI-layout library?
decisions.gist: A forward expression is normally a one-way function: you give inputs, you get an output. Reversible computation flips that — you state a relationship once and the system solves for whichever side is unknown, like spreadsheet goal-seek or a layout engine resolving sizes from constraints. The question is whether Jet adopts this as a general semantic capability, ships a narrow linear-constraint solver scoped to UI layout, or declines it and keeps plain functions + the reactive stack as the only paths.
decisions.explainer: General reversibility is a deep semantic change: an `=` would stop meaning 'bind this computed value' and start meaning 'assert this relationship, solve for the hole', which collides head-on with I8 (one canonical meaning) and forces a constraint solver into the language core. Any real solver (Z3-class SMT, or even a robust Cassowary linear solver) is a substantial dependency — in the compiler that violates I6, and even as stdlib it is heavy. The honest split: the *foundational, shippable* slice is a bounded LINEAR (Cassowary-style) solver delivered as a library scoped to UI layout, where the problem is well-posed, the math is tractable, and it slots into the reactive-UI stack already queued for Epoch 3 (D-REACTUI1) — this is a layout engine, not a language primitive, and `=` keeps its meaning everywhere. The *general* version (solve arbitrary forward constraints over arbitrary types) is open-ended research with no bounded solver and unclear semantics; it belongs post-Epoch if ever. Declining is defensible: plain functions already invert by hand, and reactive `derived` already propagates layout forward.
decisions.story: I'm building a settings panel. I write `panel = VStack.{ padding: 16 }` and a row inside it, and I want the row to fill the panel minus the padding. Today I compute that by hand: `row.width@ = panel.width.get() - 32`, and if the panel resizes I re-derive it. What I *want* is to state the relationship once — `row.width == panel.width - panel.padding*2` — pin the row's minimum, and let the layout pass solve the rest, the way Auto Layout does, so I never hand-thread which value drives which.

options.name: Decline — plain functions + reactive derived are the sanctioned paths
options.detail: Do not add reversibility or a solver as a language feature. Inverting a relationship stays an explicit, user-written function; layout that must react to inputs uses `core.reactive` (`derived`) to propagate forward. Keeps I6 (no solver dependency anywhere in the compiler), keeps I8 (`=` means one thing — bind a computed value), and keeps the surface small. Cost: layout authors hand-thread direction and hand-write any inverse; there is no goal-seek.

options.name: Foundational subset — bounded LINEAR constraint solver, library-scoped to UI layout (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship `core.layout`: a Cassowary-style incremental solver for LINEAR equalities/inequalities over numeric layout values, with weak/medium/strong/required priorities and `@suggest` edits — exactly the Auto Layout model. It is a library, not a language primitive: `=` keeps its meaning; the solver only runs inside an explicit `layout.solve.{ … }` region over declared layout values, and it ties into the reactive-UI stack (D-REACTUI1). Bounded math means a tractable, std-only implementation is realistic (no SMT). Scope is deliberately narrow — linear, numeric, layout — so it does not become a general reversibility back door (I8 honored: the one canonical job is 'resolve a layout').

options.name: Full general reversible computation / constraint solving (post-Epoch research)
options.detail: A first-class `@reversible` annotation turns a forward expression into a relation the compiler can solve in either direction over arbitrary types — goal-seek for the whole language. Requires a general solver (SMT/Z3-class), which is a hard I6 violation in the compiler and a heavy stdlib dependency, plus a deep semantic shift: `=` inside a reversible region asserts a relationship with a hole rather than binding a value (I8 tension — two meanings for one symbol). No bounded solver, undecidable in general, error/diagnostic story unsolved (rustc must never see it — I2). Powerful, but open-ended research with no clear Epoch-3 landing.

comparisons.note: The proven model for Option B: an incremental LINEAR solver with required + weak/medium/strong priorities and editable 'suggested' values. Scoped to layout, fast, well-understood, std-implementable. This is the sweet spot Jet's layout library would target.

The Option C end of the space. Janus programs run backward by construction (every statement reversible); MiniZinc/Z3 solve arbitrary constraints via a heavy external solver. Both show the cost: a solver dependency and a programming model where statements are relations, not assignments — exactly the I6 + I8 + semantic-depth problems C inherits.

decisions.title: How should Jet track taint, PII, secrets, and audited release without becoming a full IFC research language?
decisions.gist: Extend `#Tainted` to a closed label set (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`) with one taint engine and an audited declassify gate. This ballot ratifies the label taxonomy only — four follow-on ballots are required before implementation: `declassify` syntax (I7 registration), `#Sanitizer(.Kind)` specificity, sink policy declaration mechanism, and interprocedural scope. Bare `#Tainted` (D-TAINT1) must be designated sugar for `#Tainted(.Input)` with a teaching-error migration to avoid the I8 coexistence hole.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the cohesive best-in-class shape is one taint mechanism, not separate #Pii/#Secret systems and not a full Jif lattice by default. Values carry a small set of labels (`#Tainted(.Input)`, `#Tainted(.PII)`, `#Tainted(.Secret)`) that flow through existing taint propagation and are checked only at sinks. Experts get control through sink policies, org labels, audit reports, and required declassify reasons. Adversarial pass: label sets can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: built-in labels stay closed in the language; org labels live in policy; diagnostics fire at sinks, not at every assignment; full principal lattices are deferred unless Epoch 6 explicitly funds them.
decisions.story: A signup form stores an email. The web package marks it `#Tainted(.PII)`. Passing it to `log.info` fails until the developer redacts or declassifies with a reason. Security can grep every declassification and can add an org label like `.HIPAA` without changing the language.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: How can we give full control while keeping the system as small as it can be without cutting functionality? Can we turn #Tainted into something like `#Tainted(.PII)`?
Agent answer: Updated D-IFC1 around `#Tainted(.Kind)`. Best system: one taint mechanism, label set on values, built-in labels first (.Input, .PII, .Secret, .Credential), audited `declassify("reason", .Kind)`, sink policies, later org labels through policy. Devil's advocate: labels can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: closed built-ins in language, org labels only in policy, no principal lattice in Epoch 3, diagnostics at sinks only, declassification reports generated from semantic graph.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): Five concrete implementation blockers: (1) `declassify` syntactic form is undefined — must be I7-registered as a keyword or redesigned as a three-argument core library fn. (2) .Kind label type is unresolved — value-position dot requires a known expected type (D-ENUMDOT2=A); where is it declared and how does a caller use it? (3) Bare #Tainted (D-TAINT1, ratified + implemented) and `#Tainted(.Kind)` (Option B) coexist as two spellings for overlapping semantics — I8 violation with a safety hole (sink policy filtering .Input does not catch bare #Tainted). (4) `#Sanitizer fn` (D-TAINT-SAN, ratified) strips all labels, breaking label-aware declassification — a SQL sanitizer must not strip .PII. (5) Sink policy declaration mechanism is entirely absent from the ballot.

options.name: `#Tainted(.Kind)` closed label taxonomy + audited declassify gate (taxonomy decision only) (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify the label taxonomy: one taint engine, four built-in labels (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`), an audited declassify gate (static string reason required), per-label sink policies (Db/Exec/Net for `.Input`; Log/Fs/Net for `.PII`/`.Secret`). This decision ratifies ONLY the label taxonomy and opt-in scope. Four follow-on ballots are required before implementation: (1) `declassify` syntactic form — keyword or three-arg core library fn, must be I7-registered; (2) `#Sanitizer` specificity — whether `#Sanitizer fn` strips all labels or becomes `#Sanitizer(.Kind)` to preserve other labels; (3) sink policy declaration mechanism — how core library fns declare their denied-label set; (4) interprocedural scope — whether labels propagate through unannotated fn parameters. Bare `#Tainted` (D-TAINT1, ratified + implemented) becomes sugar for `#Tainted(.Input)` with a teaching-error migration; I8 gap is closed by this designation.

options.name: Label-propagating distinct-type wrappers via D-DIST1 machinery
options.detail: Define `PII<T>`, `Secret<T>`, `Input<T>` as generic distinct wrapper types (D-DIST1/D-DIST3). The label IS the type; propagation is enforced by the existing type-checker without a new sema pass. Passing `PII<String>` where `String` is expected raises E0127 (distinct-type mismatch) with no new diagnostics. Declassification is an audited method: `email.declassify("support trace") -> String`. Costs: no multi-label without a union type; generic fns over `T` must propagate label type through signatures.

options.name: Defer rich information-flow to Epoch 6
options.detail: Keep today's one-bit #Tainted/sanitizer model (D-TAINT1, ratified and implemented). In Epoch 6, revisit the full label/policy/declassify system with real compliance workloads. Ship no new label taxonomy until then.

comparisons.note: Full principal lattice. Very expressive, but annotation-heavy and not mainstream.
comparisons.code: String{Alice:} secret;

comparisons.note: Strong declassify discipline validates Jet’s audited release gate, but dynamic current-label semantics are too invasive for normal Jet.
comparisons.code: declassify secret

comparisons.note: Practical industry model: sources, sinks, sanitizers, labels. Jet can make this compile-time and type-aware instead of external analysis.
comparisons.code: source -> sanitizer -> sink

decisions.bestCurrent: Jif: Jif supports label-based information-flow control with principals and declassification, but its surface is heavy.
decisions.recommendation: Ratify `#Tainted(.Kind)` label taxonomy now; four follow-on ballots before implementation (Option A). This decision ratifies the label set and taint-engine scope only — not the syntax of declassify, #Sanitizer specificity, sink policy, or interprocedural propagation.

decisions.gist: D-VISDEFAULT1 already approved a file-scope marker. This card decides the marker spelling and whether the exception is a new private keyword or the existing per-item `pub` model inverted. It is one syntax choice; it does not reopen private-by-default as the language baseline.
decisions.story: Maya owns `core.http.server`. Almost every function in the file is public API. She wants one line at the top so the file reads like an API surface, while `parse_header_fast_path` stays private without being moved to another file.

comparisons.note: Swift supports file-scoped access and explicit public API boundaries.
comparisons.code: fileprivate func helper() {}

comparisons.note: `public`/`internal`/`private` are per declaration; no file-wide flip. Clear, but noisy for API-heavy files.
comparisons.code:
public func listen(_ port: Int) -> Server { ... }
private func parseHeaderFastPath(...) -> Header { ... }

comparisons.note: Visibility is per item (`pub`, `pub(crate)`); modules give structural grouping. No file-wide public default.
comparisons.code:
pub fn listen(port: i64) -> Server { ... }
fn parse_header_fast_path(...) -> Header { ... }

comparisons.note: Section labels (`@public`, `@private`) exist, but item position changes visibility. Jet already rejected that kind of positional surprise.

options.name: #PubFile + `priv` exceptions (recommended)
options.detail: One marker at the top flips this file to public-by-default. `priv` is the single exception keyword inside that file. Reads literally and keeps the exception local. Follow-up needed only to register `priv` in Syntax.rs and teaching errors.
options.code:
#PubFile

fn listen(port: Int) -> Server { ... }      // public
fn route(path: String) -> Route { ... }     // public
priv fn normalize_path(p: String) -> String { ... }

options.name: #PublicFile + `private` exceptions
options.detail: Same semantics, more English. `private` is longer and introduces a second visibility word beside `pub`, but it is self-explanatory for beginners.

options.name: Section labels `pub:` / `priv:`
options.detail: Lets one file mix public and private sections. Rejected as recommendation because item position becomes semantic: moving a helper above or below a label changes exports. That is the exact readability trap the file marker avoids.

decisions.recReason: `#PubFile` is short, direct, and consistent with Jet marker casing. `priv` is the smallest readable opposite of existing `pub`. Section labels are too position-sensitive.
decisions.title: What is the file-scope public-by-default marker, and how do private exceptions read?
decisions.explainer: S18 stays private-by-default. The approved marker is an opt-in escape for files that are mostly public API. The owner needs to pick two visible words: the file marker and the explicit-private exception inside that file. Avoid section markers here: S18 already rejected grouped visibility because moving an item across a line silently changes its export status. Also avoid `@` markers: D-ATTR1 retired `@` as an attribute prefix; Jet markers use `#PascalCase`/`#Name(...)`.
decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift supports file-scoped access and explicit public API boundaries.
decisions.recommendation: Use `#PubFile` with `priv` exceptions. Jet keeps private-by-default globally while giving API-heavy files a clear opt-in.

decisions.gist: Expose Cassowary-class layout as typed constraint values. Two open language gates must be resolved first: whether comparison operators may return non-Bool on closed built-in types, and whether core.layout.Var enters the compiler's closed type family. If both gates ratify, the ideal design is a static `layout { }` block (beginner face) desugaring to first-class typed constraint handles (expert layer), with axis-typed variables (`HVar`/`VVar`/`LengthVar`) that make cross-axis constraints compile errors. This is strictly better than Apple Auto Layout: readable authoring, inspectable/named/removable constraints, axis safety at compile time, and a structured conflict diagnostic rather than a runtime dump. If the language gates are declined, a method-only builder (Option A) is the safe fallback consistent with all ratified decisions.
decisions.story: Elena is building a settings panel. She wants the label column to be at least 80px wide, the input column to fill the rest, and a 16px gap between them. She writes these as constraints rather than calculated values so the layout adjusts automatically when the panel resizes.

comparisons.note: Auto Layout expresses UI constraints as linear equations and inequalities over anchors, the strongest production layout solver model.
comparisons.code: view.left == other.right + 8

options.name: `layout { }` block + typed-axis variables — gated on two language gates (recommended)
options.detail: A `layout { }` block desugars to first-class typed `Constraint` handles (each line is a named, removable, prioritizable handle). Layout variables are axis-typed: `HVar` (horizontal), `VVar` (vertical), `LengthVar` (unsigned scalar). Cross-axis constraints (`label.left >= label.height`) are compile errors — statically safe, zero-runtime-overhead axis checking; no existing constraint system offers this. Static layouts (all values comptime-known) can be solver-evaluated at compile time, emitting zero runtime solver. Expert escape: capture handles, adjust priorities, call `solver.suggest()`. GATE 1 (required): comparison operators may return non-Bool on specific closed built-in types — required for `>=`/`==`/`<=` on Var types to produce `Constraint`. GATE 2 (required): `core.layout.Var` and `core.layout.Length` enter the compiler's closed type family. If either gate is declined by the owner, fall through to Option B (method-only builder, unblocked today).

options.name: Method-only builder — no language gate (unblocked today)
options.detail: All constraints are explicit method calls: `Constraint.gte(a, b)`, `Constraint.eq(a, b)`. No comparison-operator overloading; no new compiler type family. Compatible with all ratified decisions (D-SIMD2, D-VECARITH1). Verbose relative to infix, but every constraint is a named, typed, inspectable value. Axis typing (G) can be added as a type-level distinction on top. The correct base layer for Option A's sugar if the language gates are later approved.
options.code:
c1 @= Constraint.gte(label.width, 80.px).named("label min")
c2 @= Constraint.eq_sum([label.width, Length(16.px), input.width], form.width)
solver.add([c1, c2])

options.name: Defer constraint solver to Epoch 6
options.detail: Ship only stack/grid/form presets for the UI stack now. Full Cassowary-based solver, constraint handles, and `layout { }` blocks defer to Epoch 6. Beginner presets cover common form/grid layouts without any solver dependency.
options.code:
Form.columns(label_min: 80.px, gap: 16.px)
// Epoch 6 revisit: full Cassowary solver + layout {} blocks

decisions.recReason: Infix operators on layout vars are the most ergonomic and don't require new syntax. Option B is good for tooling (inspectable constraints) but verbose. Option C needs a new compiler-blessed block (new syntax surface without clear I8 advantage over A).
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: best current practice is Cassowary/Auto Layout: linear constraints, priorities, edit variables, and conflict explanation. Jet can improve with typed `Constraint` values: math-like authoring for layout vars, but every constraint remains a named/removable/inspectable value. Adversarial pass: infix constraints can look like general operator overloading. Patch: only `core.layout.Var`/`Length` get blessed builders; ordinary user types still cannot overload operators.
decisions.bestCurrent: Apple Auto Layout: Auto Layout expresses UI constraints as linear equations and inequalities over anchors, the strongest production layout solver model.
decisions.recommendation: `layout { }` block desugaring to typed axis-safe Constraint handles — F+G combined (Option A) — gated on two owner decisions. If either gate is declined, Option B (method-only builder, no language gate) is the unblocked fallback.
decisions.title: What is Jet’s constraint-layout API surface?
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Consider the best approach currently in any language, then improve on it from a functionality & ergonomics perspective.
Agent answer: Updated. Best current model is Cassowary/Auto Layout: linear constraints, priorities, edit variables. Jet improves with typed Constraint values: math-like authoring, every constraint inspectable, removable, named, prioritized, and traceable. Devil's advocate: math operators look like global operator overloading. Patch: only core.layout.Var/Length comparison/arithmetic builders are blessed; no general user operator overloading.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIMARY BLOCKER: `>=` returning `Constraint` instead of `Bool` requires comparison-operator return-type overloading — explicitly not covered by D-SIMD2 or D-VECARITH1. This is a language-level gate, not an API choice, and must be balloted separately before Option B can be implemented. MISSING FEATURES: no conflict-resolution story — the defining pain point in all constraint systems. core.layout.Var carries no axis type, allowing cross-axis constraints that are geometrically nonsensical. STRINGLY-TYPED: `form.var('label_width')` conflicts with U13 preference — name should be inferred from the @= binding. OPTION G (typed-axis model) is the "better than any existing language" angle the ballot is missing.

decisions.gist: D-RENDERTGT1 approved a backend seam. This card decides the minimum trait between Jet UI and platform renderers: layout phases, event delivery, and paint calls. It is internal API shape, not user syntax.
decisions.story: Sophie is implementing the web backend for Jet's UI. She needs to implement the Backend trait. She wants to know: what methods does she have to implement, what data types do they pass around, and how do events flow back to Jet code?

comparisons.note: Flutter separates layout, paint, and hit testing through renderer objects.
comparisons.code: RenderObject.performLayout(); paint();

options.name: Three-phase measure-layout-paint trait (recommended)
options.detail: Backend trait has three required methods: measure(node, constraint) -> Size (phase 1), layout(node, frame) (phase 2, sets final positions), paint(node, painter) (phase 3, draws to backend surface). Events flow in via a separate on_event(event) method. This is the universal model used by Flutter, SwiftUI internals, and Yoga.

options.name: Two-phase layout-paint trait (simplified)
options.detail: Combine measure+layout into a single layout(node, available: Size) -> Rect phase. Simpler to implement but less powerful: intrinsic size information is lost after layout, making some responsive layouts impossible. Better for simple backends (TUI, fixed-size targets), worse for CSS-flexbox-style adaptive layouts.

options.name: Event-driven reactive trait
options.detail: Backend is fully event-driven: the UI framework pushes layout/paint requests as events to the backend, and the backend responds. No synchronous method calls. Aligns with async runtime and signal model but introduces significant complexity in the protocol — backends must process events in order and cannot ask the framework questions synchronously.

decisions.recReason: Three-phase is the proven industry model (Flutter, Yoga, SwiftUI internals). Backends can implement C (simplified) on top of A by merging measure+layout, but A cannot be recovered from B. The measure phase is essential for intrinsic-size-aware layout (text reflow, content-sized containers).
decisions.explainer: Group this with layout/reactive UI. The owner is choosing architectural contract, not syntax. The trait must support native widgets, browser DOM, and future custom renderers without leaking one platform into the Jet UI model.
decisions.bestCurrent: Flutter: Flutter separates layout, paint, and hit testing through renderer objects.
decisions.recommendation: Use a three-phase measure-layout-paint trait. Jet gets Flutter-grade backend portability while keeping layout decisions explicit and testable.

decisions.gist: D-NATIVEUI1 approved Phase 1: thin Jet wrapper over native platform widgets. This decides which platform to build first and whether to build all three simultaneously.
decisions.story: Derek is building a Jet desktop app. He's on macOS. He wants to ship to Windows users too. He needs the native UI backend to exist so his app can render native widgets on both platforms from the same Jet code.
decisions.comparisons: Qt: cross-platform C++ widget toolkit, all platforms simultaneously. GTK: Linux-first, cross-platform with backends. wxWidgets: wraps native APIs per platform, all platforms. Electron: web tech, all platforms simultaneously. Flutter desktop: all platforms (macOS/Win/Linux) in one unified release. Tauri: web + native, all platforms.

options.name: macOS (AppKit) first, then Windows and Linux
options.detail: Build the macOS AppKit wrapper first (narrowest FFI surface, best macOS support). The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is defined and proven against AppKit before tackling Win32/GTK. Ship macOS, then add platforms. Risk: Windows users wait; API may be too AppKit-shaped.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: macOS only
use core.ui.native  // backed by AppKit on macOS

options.name: All three platforms simultaneously (recommended)
options.detail: Build AppKit, Win32/WinUI, and GTK backends in parallel. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is kept platform-agnostic from day one. Jet's platform detection at compile time routes to the right backend. Flutter's desktop approach — commitment to parity from the start prevents API drift. Higher up-front cost but the right shape from the start.

options.name: Linux (GTK) first for CI/headless testing
options.detail: GTK is available in CI headless environments (Xvfb). Build GTK first to establish the testing infrastructure and Backend trait API with automated tests. Then port to AppKit and Win32. Best for testing rigor; not ideal for the majority macOS/Windows developer audience.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: GTK on Linux (CI-first)
use core.ui.native  // backed by GTK on Linux

decisions.recReason: Flutter's lesson: committing to cross-platform from the start produces a better API than porting a single-platform API later. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) provides the seam; parallel implementation keeps all three honest against the same contract.

decisions.gist: Partition inference requires a `Browser` effect (or equivalent named call-graph rule) as its engine — the current D-EFF4 closed set has no such entry. The JS/WASM boundary is bidirectional (WASM→JS exports and JS→WASM callbacks) and interacts with the D-SIGNAL1 reactive graph. Before this decision can be ratified, D-WEBKIND1 (WASM target) and D-JSBIND1 (boundary types) must exist as ballot cards, and the inference engine must be defined precisely enough to snapshot-test.
decisions.story: Priya writes a dashboard. Her chart view responds to clicks in the browser, but CSV export and matrix transforms should run in WASM. She does not want to annotate a hundred helper functions; she wants Jet to send pure compute to WASM and keep browser API code in JS.

comparisons.note: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.
comparisons.code: // use browser API => client bundle

options.name: Infer from `Browser` effect + allow module-level target ceilings (recommended)
options.detail: Amend D-EFF4 with a `Browser` effect and use effects as the default partition engine: browser/DOM APIs imply JS; pure/compute code is WASM-eligible. Add the useful part of B as expert control: a module may declare `#Target(Wasm)` or `#Target(Js)` as a ceiling/default, and sema validates it against the inferred effects. This keeps beginner magic (no required module declarations) and gives large teams auditable module-level placement. Per-function `#Wasm`, `#Js`, and `#WasmExport` remain overrides. GATES: D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 still need ballots before implementation.

options.name: Module-level `#Target(Wasm)` / `#Target(Js)` declarations + sema validation
options.detail: Each module declares its default compile target in the header. All functions in the module inherit the default; per-function overrides allowed. Inference validates: a `#Target(Wasm)` module calling a Browser-effect function is a compile error. Explicit, auditable, and no language-gate dependency (no comparison-operator or compiler-type-family changes required). Less magic than Option A for beginners; more auditable for large teams. Does not require amending D-EFF4. Compatible with D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 being raised later.

options.name: Defer web partitioning to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not decide the JS/WASM boundary now. D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 are unraised cards that must precede a sound partition model. D-EFF4 may need amending. D-SIGNAL1=A reactive primitives have no boundary model. D-PLUGIN1's Component Model may or may not compose with the web-backend WASM target. Deciding D-WASM1 before these gates produces a model that will be revised within the same epoch.
options.code:
// No web target partition policy yet.
// Epoch 6 revisit after D-WEBKIND1, D-JSBIND1, and D-EFF4 amendment are settled.

decisions.recReason: Effects already encode the information. Inference gives beginner magic and keeps target details out of normal Jet code; explicit markers remain possible later for exports, not partitioning every helper.
decisions.title: For the web backend, how does Jet partition JS DOM code and WASM logic while preserving expert control?
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: pure inference is not enough for experts. Best shape is inferred default plus explicit markers and a partition report. Compared with Next/SvelteKit, Jet should keep the magic boundary inference but add typed bridge/audit reports. Compared with wasm-bindgen, Jet should require less manual glue and own all diagnostics. Adversarial pass: override markers can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema rejects browser handles in WASM, checks bridgeable types/effects, emits a build manifest, and snapshots boundary diagnostics.
decisions.bestCurrent: SvelteKit / Next.js: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.
decisions.recommendation: Use effect inference by default plus module-level `#Target` controls (Option A). Pure B makes every beginner choose a target; hybrid A gives magic out of the box and expert visibility where teams need it.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: We must ensure full expert control & auditability. Reconsider this ballot with devil's advocate, make it best in the world.
Agent answer: Updated. New rec: C, not pure inference. Default is inferred from effects and browser API use; experts can pin #Wasm, #Js, #WasmExport, then inspect `jet build --target web --explain-partition`. Devil's advocate: overrides can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema checks all boundary types/effects, rejects browser handles in WASM, emits a bridge manifest, snapshots boundary diagnostics.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): INFERENCE ENGINE GAP: D-EFF4 (ratified) closed the effect vocabulary at ten effects with no Browser/Dom entry; Option C inference has no implementation foundation without amending D-EFF4 or introducing a parallel ad-hoc tracking pass (I8 violation). Option F (add Browser effect) is the I8-coherent path. PURE ≠ WASM: #Pure (empty effect set) ≠ "WASM candidate" — wasm32-wasip2 allows Net/Fs effects in WASM; correct inference rule is "no Browser effect in transitive closure," blocked on D-WEBKIND1. CALLBACK BRIDGE MISSING: #WasmExport covers WASM→JS direction only; JS→WASM callbacks are absent from all options, gated on D-JSBIND1. D-PLUGIN1 COHERENCE: D-PLUGIN1=B (WASM Component Model) and this web-backend WASM model are two distinct incompatible WASM compile targets — neither ballot acknowledges the other.

decisions.gist: Rich reflection is already approved. This card decides whether `T.reflect()` returns one typed handle with methods, a variant description you pattern-match, or trait-gated reflection. The goal is derive authors reading fields, methods, generics, and markers without raw AST access.
decisions.story: Victor writes a `Codable` derive. For each field he needs the Jet field name, type, visibility, default marker, and rename marker. He should not parse source text or inspect generated Rust; he should ask the reflected type handle.

comparisons.note: Swift exposes reflection through `Mirror`, a single value describing children/labels/types.
comparisons.code: Mirror(reflecting: value).children

options.name: One `TypeInfo` handle with typed metadata values (recommended)
options.detail: `T.reflect()` returns `TypeInfo`. It has methods like `.fields() -> [FieldInfo]`, `.methods() -> [MethodInfo]`, `.type_params()`, `.markers()`, `.implements(Trait)`. Each info value exposes typed methods, not open dictionaries.

options.name: Variant description tree
options.detail: `T.reflect()` returns a `TypeDescription` enum. Users dispatch on `.Struct`, `.Enum`, `.Primitive`, etc. This is precise, but every simple field loop starts with boilerplate.

options.name: Reflection as a trait
options.detail: Only types implementing `Reflect` expose metadata. This fits trait vocabulary, but makes reflection availability another derive/trait condition and conflicts with the goal that compiler-known type facts are always available to comptime derives.

decisions.recReason: One typed handle matches the ratified reflection direction and gives derive authors the shortest correct path. It exposes sema facts, not AST internals.
decisions.title: What shape does the typed reflection API return to comptime code?
decisions.explainer: D-METAREFLECT1 chose one reflected type handle, not AST injection. D-CTCODEGEN1 says generated code re-enters lexer/parser/sema, so reflection must expose sema-approved facts only. That means no raw parser nodes, no Rust types, and no untyped `Any` blob that makes derive authors guess. Examples use ratified Jet spellings: `comptime`, `@=` bindings, `if subject == { }` style dispatch when needed.
decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift exposes reflection through `Mirror`, a single value describing children/labels/types.
decisions.recommendation: Return one typed `TypeInfo` handle. Jet can make Swift-style reflection compile-time-only and strongly typed for derives.

decisions.gist: `#Reactive` is already the opt-in scope marker. This card decides the library vocabulary underneath it: mutable sources, derived values, and side-effect scopes. It should be one small API, not a second language.
decisions.story: Fiona writes a counter widget. `count` changes on click, `doubled` updates from `count`, and the label rerenders when either value changes. She should see exactly which values are mutable and which are derived.

comparisons.note: SolidJS has primitive signals, memos, and effects with fine-grained dependency tracking.
comparisons.code: const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0);

options.name: `Signal<T>` + `Computed<T>` + `Effect` (recommended)
options.detail: Three names for three jobs. `Signal` is mutable, `Computed` is read-only derived state, `Effect` is the runtime value created by `#Reactive`. Familiar from Preact/Solid/Vue while staying explicit.

options.name: `Cell<T>` + `derived` + `watch`
options.detail: More plain-English, spreadsheet-flavored names. Good beginner readability, but `Cell` already has meanings in Rust/interior mutability and spreadsheets; `watch` is less clearly a retained effect value.
options.code:
count @= Cell(0)
doubled @= derived(() => count.get() * 2)
watch(() => label.set_text(doubled.get().to_string()))

options.name: One `Reactive<T>` value with `.map()` / `.effect()`
options.detail: Fewer type names, but blurs mutable source, derived value, and effect lifetime. Harder diagnostics because every misuse is on one overloaded concept.
options.code:
count @= Reactive(0)
doubled @= count.map((n: Int) => n * 2)
doubled.effect((n: Int) => label.set_text(n.to_string()))

decisions.recReason: Three concrete types make dependency graph roles visible and keep diagnostics simple. `#Reactive` remains the only reactive syntax; the library handles graph mechanics.
decisions.title: What are the primitive `core.reactive` types under `#Reactive`?
decisions.explainer: Reactive code has three jobs: hold changing state, compute a value from other reactive reads, and rerun an effect when dependencies change. `#Reactive { }` should desugar to the effect job only; ordinary library types do the rest. Avoid syntax-shaped examples like `let` or operator lambdas that Jet has not ratified. This card is API naming, not new syntax.
decisions.bestCurrent: SolidJS: SolidJS has primitive signals, memos, and effects with fine-grained dependency tracking.
decisions.recommendation: Use `Signal<T>`, `Computed<T>`, and `Effect`. Jet should adopt the clearest fine-grained reactive triad and let `#Reactive` wire capture.

decisions.gist: M:N green threads are decided. This card chooses the runtime implementation behind blocking-looking socket/file APIs. It is not user syntax: user code keeps `task { }`, channels, and ordinary reads/writes.
decisions.story: Gary runs a chat server with 50,000 open TCP connections. Most sockets are idle. `socket.read()` should park the Jet task and free the OS thread until the socket is ready, without Gary learning epoll, kqueue, or IOCP.

comparisons.note: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.
comparisons.code: runtime netpoll: epoll/kqueue/IOCP

options.name: Own platform-native backends (recommended)
options.detail: Implement Linux io_uring/epoll, macOS/BSD kqueue, and Windows IOCP behind one runtime trait. No external event-loop dependency. Highest ceiling and matches Go/BEAM shape: one scheduler, native pollers, task parking, timers, cancellation, and metrics under Jet control.

options.name: Own portable poller first
options.detail: Start with epoll/kqueue/IOCP readiness only; defer `io_uring` batching. Still no external dependency and simpler to test, but leaves Linux peak throughput on the table.

options.name: Use libuv through C FFI
options.detail: Battle-tested portability. Requires explicit owner approval for a runtime external C dependency and a system-library story. Good fallback if owned backends stall, but not the best Jet identity.

decisions.recReason: Owning native backends gives Jet the highest performance ceiling, no foreign event-loop dependency, and full observability/control for the task-scope/task runtime. It keeps the user surface unchanged while letting experts tune the runtime.
decisions.title: Which OS readiness backend parks M:N tasks on I/O?
decisions.explainer: The scheduler needs one park/wake layer per platform. The decision is between owning native backends, owning a lowest-common-denominator poller, or depending on libuv. I6 matters: compiler Source has zero external crates, and runtime-side deps still need owner approval. The E3 goal is better-than-Go networking, so the backend must support task-per-connection scale, O(ready events) wakeups, low allocation pressure, and runtime observability.
decisions.bestCurrent: Go: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.
decisions.recommendation: Build own platform-native backends. Jet needs Go-class scaling as the floor and a higher ceiling through native pollers, structured cancellation, deadlines, and runtime metrics.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a structured select combinator for channels, timers, task handles, and I/O events?
decisions.gist: Select must provide a single, coherent construct that specifies what to wait for AND what to do when each arm fires. The open questions before any option is implementable: what type does the wait produce, how does the builder's lifetime bind to the taskgroup scope, and what label replaces the keyword-conflicting `as:`. A if-fused form that reuses ratified if-subject arm syntax may resolve all three without new surface.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: syntax should be cohesive with task scopes and avoid a second `case` mini-language. A scoped fluent builder keeps ownership under the nursery/taskgroup and lets losing waits deregister safely. Adversarial pass: fluent chains can get long and hide arm identity. Patch: formatter keeps one wait arm per line, every arm has an explicit result tag, and reusable select sets can become values later without new syntax.
decisions.story: I am writing a WebSocket hub. For each connection I need to react to whichever happens first: a client message, a broadcast channel message, a heartbeat timer, or server shutdown. I want one structured wait that cleans up the losing waits automatically.
decisions.inWild:
taskgroup g {
    ev @= g.select()
        .recv(inbox, as: .Message)
        .read(conn, as: .ClientData)
        .after(ms: 30_000, as: .Heartbeat)
        .cancelled(as: .Shutdown)
        .wait()?
    handle(ev)?
}
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: I like A but don't like the syntax. Please provide an updated ballot with more cohesive options and much better syntax.
Agent answer: Updated. New syntax recommendation: fluent scoped select, `g.select().recv(...).read(...).after(...).wait()?`. Avoids `case`/block syntax, keeps ownership under the taskgroup, gives each event an explicit result tag. Devil's advocate: fluent chains can get long. Patch: formatter keeps one arm per line, each arm has a stable typed result.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) `as:` label is syntactically invalid — KW_AS is a reserved keyword in Syntax.rs; every Option A example needs a different label. (2) Option A's return type is unspecified — a blocking design gap that if-fused Option F resolves by inheriting match's existing type rules. (3) .cancelled() in Option A conflicts with D-DEADLINE1=A's #Context propagation — two mechanisms for the same cancellation event. (4) Select-vs-race boundary must be drawn explicitly (I8): if `select` can race task handles, `race(handles)` is redundant. (5) Option E's Epoch 6 target is a category error; E6 = CI/docs, not language surface features; correct target is E3 after D-NURSERY1 ships.

options.name: If-fused select: `if g.select() { .recv(ch) -> val: ...; }` (recommended)
options.detail: Reuse the ratified if-subject arm syntax (S68, D-IF1, D-MATCHARM1=A, D-MATCHARM2=B) directly as the select surface. `g.select()` is the match subject; each arm names the event source and binds the result inline. Arm handlers are co-located with their declarations. Return type is the union of the arm handler return types — exactly what match already computes (no new type rule needed). Taskgroup `g` owns registration; losing arms deregister when any arm fires. No new language statement (avoids the parser cost the current ballot assigns to the `select { }` block option). No reserved-word collision (`as:` is not used — arm binding is direct in the match form). Extensibility: any type implementing a `Selectable` trait is a valid arm source. Gate: D-NURSERY1 must ship first (taskgroup/nursery primitive must exist).

options.name: Fluent `g.select().recv(...).after(...).wait()?` builder
options.detail: No new language statement; scoped to the taskgroup. Four blocking design gaps must be resolved before implementation: (1) Return type of `.wait()` — pre-declared user enum, compiler-synthesized tagged union, or match extension; (2) `as:` label must be renamed (`as` is KW_AS, reserved); (3) Builder lifetime relative to taskgroup must be specified; (4) Select/race boundary must be drawn (which sources belong here vs `race/any/all`). These resolutions tend to converge toward the if-fused form (Option A).
options.code:
ev @= g.select()
    .recv(inbox, tag: .Message)    // "as:" renamed — KW_AS is reserved
    .read(socket, tag: .Data)
    .after(ms: 50, tag: .Timeout)
    .wait()?

options.name: Defer select to after D-NURSERY1 ships
options.detail: Do not add a select API until the taskgroup/nursery primitive is implemented and the runtime's event polling model is operational. Fallback: `race/all/any` over helper tasks, which incurs task-allocation overhead and is less ergonomic. The correct defer target is Epoch 3 after D-NURSERY1 ships — not Epoch 6 (which is CI/docs, not language surface).

comparisons.note: select is central to channels, cancellation, timers, and server loops. It is powerful but a distinct language statement.
comparisons.code: select { case msg := <-ch: ...; case <-ctx.Done(): ... }

comparisons.note: tokio::select! handles futures and channels, but macro/future ceremony leaks into user code.
comparisons.code: tokio::select! { v = rx.recv() => ..., _ = sleep(d) => ... }

comparisons.note: receive expresses actor mailbox selection; great for actors, less general for typed channels, timers, and native I/O under one model.
comparisons.code: receive Msg -> handle(Msg) after 5000 -> timeout end

decisions.bestCurrent: Go select proves event choice belongs in the core concurrency toolbox; Tokio select proves the same need for async runtimes.
decisions.recommendation: If-fused select using the ratified if-subject arm syntax — no new language statement, return type resolved, no keyword conflicts (Option A). Option B (fluent builder) has four unresolved design gaps that converge on the same design anyway.

Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.title: What spelling should Jet use for the scoped task group?
decisions.gist: The model needs a lexical scope that owns child tasks, but the word `nursery` may be too borrowed and obscure. This decision chooses the final user-facing spelling.
decisions.explainer: `nursery` is precise in Trio, but it is not obvious to most programmers and does not read like Jet systems-language product copy. The concept should survive; the word should be challenged. The spelling should make three facts visible: this is about tasks, it is a group/scope, and child work is owned until scope exit. The choice must not introduce a second spawn model or imply actor supervision unless that is really what it does.
decisions.story: I am new to Jet and I see a block that spawns three API calls. I should understand from the keyword that this block owns a group of tasks and waits/cancels them at the end, without knowing Trio history.

options.name: `taskgroup g { ... }` (recommended)
options.detail: One keyword that says exactly what the construct owns: a group of tasks. It is plain, searchable, close to Swift TaskGroup terminology, and avoids importing Trio jargon. It keeps `task { }` visually related to the scoped form. Downside: compound keyword is less pretty than a short word.

options.name: `task group g { ... }`
options.detail: Most readable English and clearly related to `task`. Downside: two-word keyword phrase adds parser/teaching weight and can look like a declaration rather than a control construct.

options.name: `scope g { ... }`
options.detail: Short and general. Downside: too vague; Jet will have many scopes, and this hides that the construct owns concurrent tasks.

options.name: `nursery n { ... }`
options.detail: Best-known term in structured-concurrency literature through Trio. Downside: obscure to non-Trio users, not self-describing, and product-language mismatch for Jet.

options.name: `with tasks g { ... }`
options.detail: Reads naturally and emphasizes a scoped region. Downside: adds or overloads `with`; less direct as a named API receiver for combinators.

comparisons.note: TaskGroup is mainstream and directly names the idea: a group of child tasks with scoped lifetime.
comparisons.code: withTaskGroup(of: T.self) { group in ... }

comparisons.note: Nursery is semantically strong but jargon-heavy outside Trio.
comparisons.code: async with trio.open_nursery() as nursery:

comparisons.note: coroutineScope is accurate but tied to coroutine vocabulary Jet is intentionally hiding from beginners.
comparisons.code: coroutineScope { async { ... } }

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift TaskGroup has the clearest mainstream name; Trio nursery has the strongest semantics but weaker product language.
decisions.recommendation: Use `taskgroup g { ... }` unless the owner prefers another spelling. It keeps the task relationship obvious and avoids Trio-specific vocabulary.

decisions.title: Should workspace resolution write a separate `.jet/workspace.lock` or fold into unified `.jet/lock`?
decisions.gist: Workspace member discovery needs one durable lock location. A separate workspace lock duplicates package locking; a unified `.jet/lock` keeps one source of reproducibility truth.
decisions.explainer: D-WORKSPACE1/B chose `pack.jet payload:` instead of a new `workspace.jet` file, so the lock should follow the same I8 logic: one package/workspace graph, one lock. The only reason to split is if workspace member discovery has a different lifecycle from dependency resolution. Splitting creates two files CI must validate and two stale states users must debug.
decisions.story: Mara opens a monorepo and runs `jet test`. She wants one lockfile checked into review that tells CI exactly which payload members and dependencies were used, without learning whether a change belongs in package lock or workspace lock.
decisions.inWild:
# pack.jet
[payload]
members = find("./packages")

# recommended lock result:
.jet/lock   # contains dependency pins plus normalized payload-member graph

options.name: Fold workspace graph into unified `.jet/lock` (recommended)
options.detail: One `.jet/lock` file stores dependency pins, payload member paths (normalized), sparse-subtree metadata, and comptime member-expression inputs. Matches D-WORKSPACE1=B: no new workspace file, no new lock file. CI validates one lock with `jet fetch --locked`. Consistent with Cargo (one Cargo.lock for the whole workspace) and pnpm (one pnpm-lock.yaml). When the member expression is a comptime `find()`, the lock records the discovered paths so future builds are hermetic without re-evaluating the expression.
options.code:
# pack.jet
[payload]
members = find("./packages")

# .jet/lock  (one file covers everything)
[workspace]
members = ["packages/a", "packages/b"]  # normalized from find() at lock time

[deps]
core = "1.4.2"

$ jet fetch --locked  # validates both sections

options.name: Separate `.jet/workspace.lock`
options.detail: Workspace member discovery gets its own lock file, distinct from `.jet/lock` which covers dependencies. Isolates member-list churn from dep pins, but creates two sources of truth and two failure modes under `--locked`. Reviewers must understand which lock to check for which change.
options.code:
.jet/lock           # dependency pins
.jet/workspace.lock  # member paths

options.name: Defer member-expression locking — explicit lists only for now
options.detail: Support only explicit member lists (no `find()`/comptime discovery) until D-CTMARKER1/D-CTEFFECT1 implementation lands. Avoids choosing lock shape for computed members now. Blocks the full D-WORKSPACE1=B surface.
options.code:
# only explicit members for now
[payload]
members = ["packages/a", "packages/b"]
# Epoch 3 revisit: find() members + .jet/lock recording

comparisons.note: One Cargo.lock records the whole workspace dependency graph, not a separate workspace lock.
comparisons.code: Cargo.lock

comparisons.note: One pnpm-lock.yaml includes workspace package graph and dependency resolution together.
comparisons.code: pnpm-lock.yaml

decisions.bestCurrent: Cargo/pnpm: one lockfile covers the complete workspace graph.
decisions.recommendation: Fold workspace member graph into unified `.jet/lock` — one reproducibility file, one CI gate (Option A). I8: one lock mechanism covers both dependency pins and payload-member discovery.

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: What is the ratified syntax and access gate for labeled stored-reference fields?
decisions.gist: Stored reference fields let structs carry zero-copy views into owner values; owner selected marker syntax `#Ref(Label)`.
decisions.explainer: The recovered #100 concern is not an unresolved dangling-reference bug. E2-M5 hardened stored refs. The remaining issue is governance: `ref[label] field: T` is user-typeable, documented by diagnostics, and absent from syntax-decisions.md. I7 requires every keyword/sigil to have a decision ID. This ballot either ratifies that syntax, replaces it, or removes it until a better tier-2 stored-reference model exists.
decisions.story: Earl builds a parser over a large input buffer. He wants tokens and slices to point into that buffer without allocating new strings, while the compiler still proves the buffer outlives every view.

options.name: Ratify `ref[label] field: T` behind `use core.mem` (recommended)
options.detail: Purpose: this is for structs that store a view into another value, e.g. parser tokens pointing into an input buffer, graph edges pointing into arena-owned nodes, or zero-copy packet/header views. The normal Jet memory model lets functions borrow during a call, but v1 intentionally disallows storing/returning references in beginner code. `ref[label] field: T` is the expert-tier opt-in that exposes that power while naming the owner relationship. It does not make unsafe memory possible by itself; sema must still reject dangling/escaping views. Gate it behind `use core.mem` so beginners never encounter stored-reference vocabulary accidentally.

options.name: `#Ref(Label)` field marker, no import gate (ratified)
options.detail: Stored reference fields use normal Jet marker syntax on the field: `#Ref(arena) name: T`. The label names the owner relationship sema must prove. No `use core.mem` gate is required per owner choice; safety still comes from sema rejecting dangling or escaping views. This gives experts zero-copy stored views that call-time `&`/`~` capabilities cannot express, while avoiding a new bracket keyword form.

options.name: Remove labeled ref fields until tier-2 references are redesigned
options.detail: Delete or hide current syntax and diagnostics until a full tier-2 stored-reference model is designed. Avoids ratifying a syntax that may need to change when the broader owned/borrowed reference system (post-v1) is specified. Breaks existing examples and tests that use `ref[label]`.
options.code: // no stored reference fields until tier-2 reference model is designed

comparisons.note: Rust encodes stored-reference relationships with lifetimes; Jet intentionally has no lifetime syntax in v1.
comparisons.code: struct View<'a> { bytes: &'a [u8] }

comparisons.note: Swift mostly avoids stored borrowed references in safe user code; ownership features are explicit advanced syntax.
comparisons.code: borrow / consuming annotations

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust proves stored references need explicit relationship tracking; Jet should keep that explicit but hide it behind an expert gate.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: use `#Ref(Label)` on the field, with no `use core.mem` gate (Option B as amended).

log.text: Owner amendment applied: stored-ref fields use `#Ref(Label)` syntax.
Owner asked purpose/control question; ballot expanded to explain zero-copy stored views and why call-time capabilities are insufficient.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.comment: Use syntax `#Ref(Label)` instead of `ref[label]`; no import gate.

decisions.title: Reopen C FFI syntax or keep S59/D-CFFI2-SYN?
decisions.gist: C FFI syntax is already ratified. This decides whether `#Lang_C`-style blocks are better enough to reopen that surface.
decisions.explainer: C FFI syntax is already ratified. This decides whether `#Lang_C`-style blocks are better enough to reopen that surface. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A systems programmer binds a small C header. They want the boundary to read clearly as C interop without importing C syntax into normal Jet code.

options.name: Keep C FFI, but spell blocks `#Extern module` (ratified)
options.detail: Keep the ratified C FFI model (`use c.<lib> as alias`, generated bindings, same safety gates) but update the marker spelling to Jet-canonical `#Extern module`, per owner comment. This preserves one C-binding mechanism while aligning with PascalCase marker syntax; `@extern` becomes retired teaching syntax.

options.name: Add `#Lang_C { ... }` C-FFI block
options.detail: A marker block visually names the foreign language. Risk: looks like a syntax island and may imply raw C declarations parse inside Jet braces (they do not). I8 concern: `#Lang_C { }` and `@extern module` both declare C bindings — two mechanisms for one job. Only justified if user research shows `@extern module` is consistently misread.

options.name: Docs-only: teach "C binding block" terminology without new syntax
options.detail: Keep current syntax; rename the docs section and examples to use "C binding block" as the teaching term. No syntax change, no I8 cost. Correct if the issue is terminology, not syntax.
options.code:
// docs: "C binding block"
@extern module libc { fn puts(s: *U8) -> Int }

comparisons.note: Existing ratified decisions are the baseline; reopening needs a clear safety/readability win.
comparisons.code: see docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: keep the existing C FFI model, but spell the binding block `#Extern module`, not `@extern module`.

log.text: Owner ratified A with amendment: use `#Extern` instead of `@extern`; option text updated.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a compact counted-loop header with semicolon-separated parts?
decisions.gist: The question is not `for` as an alias; it is whether loop setup, bound, and increment need a compact header form.
decisions.explainer: Jet already chose one `loop` keyword and no visible semicolons. This decides whether Odin-style `for`/`;` loop headers are worth reopening. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: Hank writes a byte scanner. He wants one line to name the index, set its bounds, and say how it advances. A beginner should still understand which part starts the loop, which part stops it, and which part changes each turn.
decisions.inWild:
loop i in 0..len step 4 { scan(bytes[i]) }

loop i := 0; i < len; i += 4 { scan(bytes[i]) }

options.name: Keep range + `step` as the compact counted loop (recommended)
options.detail: Preserve the ratified shape: `loop i in start..end step n`. It already gives a one-line iterator variable, range, and increment for the common counted-loop case, without making semicolons user-visible. More complex state changes stay in the loop body where they are explicit.

options.name: Add a semicolon header under `loop`
options.detail: Keep Jet's `loop` keyword, but allow a C/Odin-style counted header: initializer; condition; afterthought. Semicolons would be legal only inside this header, not as statement separators. This gives experts compact control over non-range increments, but it creates a second counted-loop mechanism beside `loop i in range step n`.

options.name: Add a named-header form without semicolons
options.detail: Use labels inside the loop header instead of punctuation: `from`, `while`, and `step` name the same three jobs. This keeps visible semicolons out of Jet, but adds new contextual words and still overlaps with the current range form.

options.name: Expert-only counted loop marker
options.detail: Keep beginner loops unchanged and put arbitrary counted headers behind an explicit expert marker, e.g. `#Counted loop init; cond; step`. This surfaces the control when needed without making it the everyday loop form, but it is heavier and still spends semicolon syntax.

comparisons.note: One `loop` keyword; counted loops use inclusive ranges and `step`.
comparisons.code: loop i in 0..10 step 2 { print(i) }

comparisons.note: Initializer, condition, and afterthought share one header separated by semicolons.
comparisons.code: for i := 0; i < 10; i += 2 { print(i) }

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Keep `loop i in range step n` as the compact counted-loop path (Option A). It already carries iterator, bounds, and increment in one line while preserving Jet's no-visible-semicolon rule. Option B is the direct answer if the owner wants full C/Odin header control.

log.text: Owner clarified the proposal: semicolon-separated loop header parts, not a `for` alias. Ballot rebuilt around compact counted-loop syntax.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet support switch/case fallthrough?
decisions.gist: Jet rejected C-style `switch`/`case` and uses multi-arm `if`. This decides whether fallthrough exists at all or grouped arms are the only path.
decisions.explainer: Jet rejected C-style `switch`/`case` and uses multi-arm `if`. This decides whether fallthrough exists at all or grouped arms are the only path. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A C programmer wants two HTTP status codes to share handling. Jet should make the shared handling obvious without hidden control flow from one arm into the next.

options.name: No fallthrough; shared handling via grouped arms (recommended)
options.detail: Jet's multi-arm if syntax (`400 | 404 -> handle_client()`) handles all cases where C fallthrough is used for shared logic — with no implicit fall-through, no hidden control flow, and exhaustiveness checked. Do not add `fallthrough`. Teaching: when a C programmer asks "how do I fall through?", the diagnostic or docs point to the grouped-arm form. This is unambiguously the safer, cleaner path.

options.name: Explicit `fallthrough` statement
options.detail: Allow an arm to jump into the next arm only when it writes `fallthrough`. Familiar to switch users who expect it, but adds a second control-flow edge (arms can now have two exits), complicates exhaustiveness analysis, and reintroduces a class of bugs (wrong arm order changes behavior silently). Only justified if a use case cannot be expressed with grouped arms — which has not been demonstrated.
options.code:
400 -> { log("client"); fallthrough }
404 -> handle_client()

options.name: Reopen `switch/case/default` with fallthrough semantics
options.detail: Bring back switch vocabulary, case arms, and optional fallthrough. Conflicts with S24/D-IF1 teaching policy, adds a third pattern-dispatch surface (I8), and brings C fallthrough's bug class back into the language. Not recommended under any circumstances — this is the pattern Jet's multi-arm if was designed to replace.

comparisons.note: Existing ratified decisions are the baseline; reopening needs a clear safety/readability win.
comparisons.code: see docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: No fallthrough — grouped arms (`400 | 404 -> ...`) cover all shared-handling use cases safely (Option A). C-style fallthrough is a well-documented footgun; Jet eliminated it intentionally.

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Does Jet need general union types or `Any`, and how should dynamic cases be served?
decisions.gist: Jet already has enums, optionals, fallible values, generics, traits, and data values. This decides whether to add a general dynamic escape or keep unions closed and explicit.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has enums, optionals, fallible values, generics, traits, and data values. This decides whether to add a general dynamic escape or keep unions closed and explicit. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A library author parses JSON and plugin messages. Some values are only known at runtime, but most app code should stay statically typed and beginner-safe.

options.name: No general `Any`; document the correct mechanism per use case (recommended)
options.detail: Jet already has: closed unions via enums (JSON parsing, plugin messages), polymorphism via traits/generics (algorithm abstraction), absence via T? and T?E, and data values (DataTree from D-SERDE2) for truly dynamic untyped trees. A general `Any` top type adds a second optional-like mechanism (I8) and a second polymorphism mechanism (I8), while weakening static guarantees for beginners. The correct path: a compiler diagnostic that recognizes "I need to hold anything" patterns and points at the right tool for the specific use case.

options.name: Closed union type syntax
options.detail: A type-level syntax for a fixed set of alternatives: `Int | String`. More compact than defining an enum for short-lived unions. Risk: overlaps with enum (I8: two ways to define closed unions), and pattern matching rules must extend to the union form. Only justified if enum definition for 2-3 variant unions is demonstrably too verbose in common code.

options.name: `Any` only at interop/dynamic-data boundaries (expert-gated)
options.detail: A boxed dynamic value (like DataTree but for arbitrary types) gated behind `use core.interop`. Required explicit downcast before use; compile error outside interop scope. The narrowest possible escape hatch for FFI/plugin/serde edges. Distinct from D (full Any): upcasting to Any requires explicit invocation; the beginner surface is untouched. Only justified if DataTree + enums provably cannot cover a critical interop use case.

comparisons.note: `any` is the default escape for JS interop and gradual migration; `unknown` is the safer closed form requiring narrowing before use.
comparisons.code:
function handle(x: any) { return x.foo }  // no error
function safe(x: unknown) { return (x as {foo: string}).foo }

comparisons.note: Pre-generics, `interface{}`/`any` was the only way to write generic containers and JSON boundaries; post-generics it shrank but never disappeared at FFI/JSON edges.
comparisons.code:
var m map[string]any
json.Unmarshal(raw, &m)

comparisons.note: `Any`/`AnyObject` for heterogeneous collections and ObjC interop; app code is encouraged toward typed enums/protocols instead.
comparisons.code:
let items: [Any] = [1, "hi", UIView()]
let n = items[0] as? Int

comparisons.note: No std `Any` top type for years; `dyn Trait` for open polymorphism, `enum`/`serde_json::Value` for closed/dynamic data. `Box<dyn Any>` exists but is niche (type-id downcasts).
comparisons.code:
enum Value { Null, Bool(bool), Number(f64), String(String) }
// or trait objects: Box<dyn Display>

comparisons.note: `Any`/`Object` is the root of the class hierarchy — every reference type is implicitly an `Any`, which powers collections and reflection but erases static guarantees.
comparisons.code:
val list: List<Any> = listOf(1, "x")
val s = list[1] as String

comparisons.note: Dynamic trees via `Data`/`DataTree`; closed sums via enums (+ ratified `A | B` unions); open polymorphism via traits/generics; absence via `T?`; interop stays explicit.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: No general `Any` — existing mechanisms (enums, traits, generics, T?, data values) cover all dynamic cases without a top type (Option A).

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.
Owner question q5lq42z answered: cross-language Any survey, benefits/detriment analysis, devil's advocate pass. Comparisons facet expanded.

decisions.title: Keep Jet fallback control flow or add an Odin-style `or_` suite?
decisions.gist: Odin has a family of `or_` control operators; this maps each case to today's Jet and decides whether Jet needs another family.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has `?? return` for fallback/early return. This decides whether an Odin-style `or_return` spelling adds clarity or just a second way to mean it. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: Mara writes a log shipper. Missing config should use a default, bad records should skip the current loop turn, a closed stream should break the loop, and startup failure should return from the function. She needs the error path to stay visible without learning four unrelated spellings.

options.name: Keep Jet's existing fallback/control suite (recommended)
options.detail: Do not add Odin-style `or_` words. Jet already covers the suite with one fallback operator plus control words: value fallback is `x ?? default`, early return is `x ?? return value`, loop break is `x ?? break`, loop continue is the ratified loop shorthand `x?continue`, and normal propagation remains `x?`. The only rough edge is documentation: the ballot now names the whole map so users are not left comparing only `or_return`.

options.name: Unify all local exits under `?? <control>`
options.detail: Keep `??` as the single fallback operator, but complete the control-word family so loop skip is `x ?? continue` instead of the special `?continue`. Then fallback, return, break, and continue all read as "use the value, or do this control action." This is the most Jet-shaped path if the current `?continue` shorthand feels like an exception.

options.name: Add explicit `or_*` keywords as teaching-only diagnostics
options.detail: Reserve/recognize `or_return`, `or_break`, `or_continue`, and `or_else` only to emit teaching errors that point at the Jet spelling. No accepted second spelling reaches formatted source. This helps Odin users migrate while preserving I8.

decisions.title: How are component accessibility roles inferred, specified, and overridden?
decisions.gist: A11y-by-default should combine beginner magic with expert control: built-in components infer roles automatically, custom interactive components must declare or derive a typed role, and experts can override deliberately.
decisions.story: Walter ships a form. Standard Button/Dialog/Menu controls should be keyboard-correct with no ceremony. When he builds a custom icon-only control, Jet should infer what it safely can, require an explicit role when inference is ambiguous, and give experts a typed override path instead of raw string ARIA.

Button.{ label: "Save", on_click: save }              // built-in role: button
IconButton.{ icon: .Trash, on_click: delete }       // inferred interactive, may need label

component ToolbarToggle { ... }                     // explicit expert override

options.name: Built-in inference + explicit typed override (recommended)
options.detail: Combine A and B: core components carry fixed role/keyboard behavior; simple custom components get conservative inference from typed properties/events; ambiguous custom interactive components must use a typed role/keyboard marker. Experts can override through audited typed APIs, not raw ARIA strings. Release lint blocks missing accessible names, focus behavior, or invalid role/property combinations.
options.code:

IconButton.{ icon: .Trash, label: "Delete", on_click: delete } // inferred button + required accessible name

component ThemeToggle {
    checked: Bool
    on_toggle: fn(Bool)
}
