decisions.title: Retire S25 `||` comparison-distribution shorthand?
decisions.gist: Ratify that `||` no longer distributes comparisons; comparator value alternatives use single `|` (`x == 1 | 2`) in arm heads, while `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` remain boolean arm conditions.
decisions.explainer:
S25 was ratified on 2026-06-11 as “comparison distribution”: inside a boolean chain, a bare value to the right of a comparison reused the nearest comparison on its left. The old spelling used boolean operators, e.g. `status == 400 || 404` meant `status == 400 || status == 404`. This ballot retires that `||`/`&&` distribution rule.

Ratified shape: single `|` is the value/pattern-alternative separator against the comparator, e.g. `status == 400 | 404 ->` in an arm head. `||` and `&&` do not distribute comparisons; they combine full boolean expressions/guards. `==` and `!=` remain explicit boolean comparisons/guards in arm heads.
decisions.story: A reader sees `status == 400 || 404` and should not have to know that `404` secretly reuses `status ==`. Retiring S25 makes `||` a boolean operator only. The compact comparator-alternate form is still available where Jet pattern matching lives: `status == 400 | 404 ->` or, under an inferred comparator, `400 | 404 ->`.

options.name: Retire S25 `||` distribution (recommended)
options.detail: Delete comparison distribution from `||`/`&&`. Write full boolean comparisons in ordinary expressions. Keep single `|` for value/pattern alternatives against the comparator in arm heads, and keep `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` as boolean condition syntax inside arm heads.

options.name: Keep S25 expression shorthand
options.detail: Allow bare values in `||`/`&&` chains to reuse the nearest comparison. Compact, but `||`/`&&` would carry a Jet-only value-distribution rule instead of being boolean-only. Arm `|` alternatives and arm boolean guards still stay exactly as described above.

options.name: Retire S25 and design membership later
options.detail: Remove S25 `||`/`&&` distribution now, then separately decide whether Jet needs `in`/set/range membership sugar for common equality lists. This still preserves arm `|` alternatives and arm boolean guards.

comparisons.note: D-MATCHARM1/2 uses single `|` for alternatives against the comparator in arm heads and `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` for boolean arm conditions; retiring S25 keeps that compact arm syntax but removes hidden comparison reuse from `||`/`&&`.
Boolean operators combine Bool expressions only; repeated comparisons are explicit unless a separate membership operator exists.
comparisons.code: status == 400 || status == 404

decisions.comment: Owner ratified: retire S25 `||`/`&&` comparison distribution; comparator alternatives are single `|` (`x == 1 | 2`), not `||`.

decisions.gist: Docs/tests drift between Serialize/Deserialize language from other ecosystems and Jet’s Codable/Encode/Decode vocabulary.
decisions.explainer: Docs/tests drift between Serialize/Deserialize language from other ecosystems and Jet’s Codable/Encode/Decode vocabulary.

#[Codable]
#[Encode]
#[Decode]

decisions.title: Counted loop separator: what replaces semicolons?
decisions.gist: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C retired semicolons from counted loop headers; pick the replacement separator.
decisions.explainer: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C kept compact counted loops but deferred the separator choice. The ratified S6-R law bans visible semicolons; we need a different separator for the three-part header (init; condition; afterthought).
decisions.story: Gerald is porting a tight inner loop from C and wants the three-part form. He knows Jet has no semicolons, so he needs to know exactly what punctuation to type between the init, condition, and step.

comparisons.note: Semicolons in for-loop header
Semicolons in for-loop header
comparisons.code: for i := 0; i < n; i++ {}

comparisons.note: No three-part for; use while
comparisons.code: var i = 0; while i < n { i += 1 }

options.name: Comma separator (recommended)
options.detail: Use commas between the three parts. Commas already appear in function call arguments and tuple construction; reusing them here keeps the punctuation vocabulary small. The header reads left-to-right with natural pauses.
options.code:
loop i := 0, i < n, i += 1 { process(buf[i]) }
loop i := len, i > 0, i -= 1 { drain(q[i]) }

options.name: Keyword separators (while/step)
options.detail: Use keywords: . Self-documenting but verbose; adds two reserved words or repurposes existing ones.
options.code: loop i := 0 while i < n step i += 1 { process(buf[i]) }

options.name: Retire three-part form entirely
options.detail: Remove the three-part header. All counted loops use range iteration  or manual . Porting C loops requires rewriting them as range loops.

log.text: Raised as follow-up to D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C (redesign counted loop separator).
Closed as superseded — D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 reversed to A (keep semicolons).

decisions.comment: Superseded: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 reversed to A — semicolons stay. No separator redesign needed.

decisions.title: Ratify the two language gates required for D-LAYOUT1 option A?
decisions.gist: D-LAYOUT1=A needs two compiler extensions: comparison ops that return Constraint on layout types, and axis-typed layout variables in the closed type family.
decisions.explainer: D-LAYOUT1 ratified option A (typed-axis layout block) conditionally on two compiler language gates. If both gates are ratified here, the full design ships. If either is declined, core.layout falls back to a method-only builder (D-LAYOUT1 option B), which is implementable today without any language change.
decisions.story: Sandra is building a form layout. She wants to write  and have Jet catch  (cross-axis mix) as a compile error. Both features require the compiler to treat layout variable types specially.

comparisons.note: Uses NSLayoutConstraint builder; no axis safety
comparisons.code: label.widthAnchor.constraint(greaterThanOrEqualToConstant: 80).isActive = true

comparisons.note: frame/padding modifiers; no constraint model
comparisons.code: label.frame(minWidth: 80)

options.name: Ratify both gates — ship full typed-axis layout (recommended)
options.detail: GATE 1: comparison operators (>=, ==, <=) may return Constraint (not Bool) when both operands are closed layout variable types (HVar, VVar, LengthVar). Like D-SIMD2's closed-operator blessing, this is limited to the compiler-provided family only. GATE 2: HVar, VVar, LengthVar, Constraint, and LayoutHandle enter the compiler's closed type family (recognized by core_type_known). Both gates are tightly scoped and follow existing precedent (SIMD/D-SIMD2, distinct types/D-DIST2).

options.name: Decline gates — use method-only builder
options.detail: Keep comparison operators Bool-only and keep the closed type family as-is. core.layout ships as a method-only builder (no layout {} block, no axis safety). Implementable today with no language change. Axis errors are runtime conflicts, not compile errors.

log.text: Raised as follow-up to D-LAYOUT1=A (two language gates required to implement full design).

decisions.title: External inherent method spelling
decisions.gist: Pick the syntax for adding methods to a type outside its definition block.
decisions.story: Betty is writing a geometry library. She defines Point in geometry/types.jet and wants to add a dist() method in geometry/ops.jet without reopening the original file. What does she write?

options.name: Keep S83 ~~: fn Point~~dist(self, other: Point)
options.detail: S83 ratified ~~ for ALL external defs. D-IMPLDOT1 retired it for trait-impls only. Keeping it here means two external connectors exist: ~~ for inherent methods, . for trait impls. Single unusual token users must memorize.

options.name: fn Point.dist(self, other: Point) — mirrors D-IMPLDOT1 (recommended)
options.detail: Uses the same . connector D-IMPLDOT1 chose for impl Point.Trait. One external-attach connector for everything: inherent methods, trait impls, forwarding. fn keyword + PascalCase type name prevents any ambiguity with a call (p.dist()) — a call cannot have a capital first segment.

options.name: extend Point { fn dist(self, other: Point) }
options.detail: Groups methods in a named block like Swift extension or Kotlin companion. Clear at a glance. Adds a second block keyword beside impl — users must now pick between extend Type {} and impl Type.Trait {}, two block forms that look similar.

options.name: No external inherent methods — trait impls only
options.detail: Conflicts with ratified philosophy.md which explicitly says inline and external are two entry points of one feature. Not recommended.
options.code: // blocked — users must define all methods in the struct body or use a trait

decisions.title: How comptime block exposes values for runtime splice
decisions.gist: Does a comptime {} block expose its computed values to runtime code via $name?
decisions.story: Earl is building a tiny VM. He wants to compute an opcode dispatch table size at compile time inside a comptime {} block, then use that constant in runtime code — checked at the call site — via a $TABLE_SIZE splice.

options.name: Block-local comptime bindings leak into the enclosing scope (recommended)
options.detail: Consistent with how comptime if already works (D-WHEN1): bindings defined in comptime if arms are visible after. The block is erased at codegen; only the serialized literals from $name splices appear in output. Scope leak is bounded to comptime bindings declared directly in the block body.

options.name: Explicit expose NAME inside block marks which values escape
options.detail: Most explicit about what crosses the build/runtime boundary. Introduces a second way to declare visibility inside a block (alongside comptime NAME).

options.name: $name stays comptime-only; block exposes nothing
options.detail: Conservative — comptime {} remains a build-time assertion/side-effect block only. $name keeps working inside derive bodies and comptime binding RHS but not in runtime code. The feature is mostly already shipped.

decisions.comparisons:
Zig:       comptime { const N = 64; }  // comptime vars always accessible in enclosing scope
Rust:      const N: usize = 64;          // top-level const, no block scoping
C++:       constexpr int N = 64;         // same — top-level
Nim:       const N {.compileTime.} = 64  // pragma-gated but still top-level
D:         enum N = 64;                  // compile-time constant, no block

decisions.title: UI tree node shape: typed enum vs dynamic record
decisions.gist: Should UI view-model nodes be a typed enum (Text, Box, Button) or a dynamic tagged record?
decisions.story: Dorothy is building a to-do app. She needs text labels, containers, buttons, and input fields. She wants the compiler to catch a typo in a node kind at build time, not at runtime.

options.name: Typed constructors: ui.text(), ui.box(), ui.button() (recommended)
options.detail: Each node kind is a distinct constructor. The compiler knows statically that ui.button() produces a button node and ui.text() produces a text node. No stringly-typed fields, no runtime kind-check. Consistent with closed-type direction.

options.name: Dynamic tagged record: ui.node({ kind: "text", content: "..." })
options.detail: A single ui.node() function accepts a record with a "kind" string field. Flexible for dynamic node creation but kind typos are runtime errors. Inconsistent with Jet's static-safety direction.

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:      Text("hello") / VStack { ... } / Button("ok") {}  — typed constructors, each is a distinct type
Flutter:      Text("hello") / Column(children:[...]) / ElevatedButton(...)  — same pattern
React JSX:    <Text>hello</Text> / <View> / <Pressable>  — tagged strings compiled to typed calls
HTML:         <div> / <span> / <button>  — string tags, no compile-time kind checking
Android XML:  android:layout_width="match_parent"  — string attributes

decisions.title: Style API shape: flat record vs builder chain
decisions.gist: Should ui.Style be a flat value record or a builder-method chain?
decisions.story: Walter is styling a submit button: red background, white text, 12px padding, 80px wide. He wants to define the style as a reusable constant and pass it to multiple buttons.

options.name: Flat value record: Style { color: rgb(255,0,0), width: px(80) } (recommended)
options.detail: Style is a pure value — comparable, hashable, passable as a constant. Consistent with Jet's value semantics: no mutable builder state, no object identity, no method chain side effects. A partial style (only some fields set) uses default values for the rest.

options.name: Builder chain: Style.new().color(rgb(255,0,0)).width(px(80))
options.detail: Familiar from many UI frameworks but introduces mutable builder state. A Style mid-chain is not a value — you cannot store it, compare it, or pass it without calling a terminating method. Inconsistent with Jet's value-oriented surface.
options.code:
// Not easily reusable as a constant:
SUBMIT_STYLE #= Style.new()
    .background(rgb(220, 38, 38))
    .color(rgb(255, 255, 255))
    .padding(px(12))
    .width(px(80))
    .build()   // or is this the value? when is it a value?

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:     Text("hi").foregroundColor(.red).frame(width: 80)  — builder chain on the node, not style
Flutter:     TextStyle(color: Colors.red, fontSize: 16)              — flat struct
CSS:         { background: red; width: 80px; padding: 12px }        — flat key-value
Tailwind:    "bg-red-500 text-white p-3 w-20"                       — string class list
React:       {{ backgroundColor: 'red', width: 80, padding: 12 }}   — plain object
SwiftUI (StyleSheet): not idiomatic — styles via modifiers on views

decisions.title: Motion timing: injectable Clock vs global time signal
decisions.gist: Does core.motion.spring() take a Clock capability parameter, or does it read a global time signal?
decisions.story: Doris is building a loading spinner that animates with a spring. She needs to write a unit test that asserts the spinner reaches its target position after 300ms — without waiting 300 real milliseconds.

options.name: Injectable Clock: spring(target, clock, stiffness, damping) (recommended)
options.detail: Clock is passed in explicitly. Tests inject FakeClock.new() and call clock.advance(ms) for deterministic results. Production code passes the real system clock. Consistent with D-DET1 (all time/randomness is injectable). Flutter uses the same pattern (TickerProvider).

options.name: Global time signal: core.motion.time_signal() read internally
options.detail: Motion reads a module-level time signal automatically. Simpler call site but tests must stub the global, which requires framework-level mocking support (jest.useFakeTimers equivalent). Less consistent with D-DET1.

decisions.comparisons:
React Spring:   useSpring({ from: {x:0}, to: {x:1} })          — global RAF/time; not testable without mocking
Framer Motion:  useAnimate(), animate(el, {x:1}, {duration:0.3}) — global time; testing needs jest fake timers
SwiftUI:        withAnimation(.spring()) { state = 1 }           — global CADisplayLink; XCTest uses waitFor
GSAP:           gsap.to(el, {x:1, ease:"elastic.out"})          — global ticker; test with gsap.ticker.tick()
Flutter:        AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: ...)  — vsync injected via TickerProvider (close to option A)

decisions.title: A11y diagnostic gating mechanism
decisions.gist: How are accessibility diagnostics triggered — automatic on --release, explicit jet lint --a11y, or per-file #A11yStrict?
decisions.story: Hank's team ships a web app. He wants his CI to catch missing ARIA roles and unlabeled buttons before they reach users. But he doesn't want beginners running jet build to see a wall of a11y warnings on their first hello-world.

options.name: --release build flag enables a11y lints automatically
options.detail: Hank runs jet build --release for production and a11y lints fire automatically. But a beginner who runs jet build --release for their first deployed app also sees a wall of a11y errors on components they didn't write. Surprise on first real build.
options.code:
jet build --release
# output includes:
# W2930: button "X" has no accessible label (E2930)
# W2931: ui.text used as interactive element without role (E2931)
# 2 accessibility warnings — use --no-a11y to suppress

jet build              # no a11y lints (dev builds)
jet build --release    # a11y lints fire automatically

options.name: jet lint --a11y explicit separate step (recommended)
options.detail: A11y linting is an explicit step Hank adds to CI. It never surprises beginners. Consistent with existing lint profile pattern — same as running jet lint --unused or jet lint --style.
options.code:
# CI pipeline (Hank adds this step):
jet lint --a11y

# output:
# src/nav.jet:3: W2930: button "X" has no accessible label
# src/nav.jet:4: W2931: interactive text missing role
# 2 accessibility issues

# Beginner dev loop:
jet build     # no a11y lints — not surprised
jet run       # no a11y lints
jet lint      # base lints only
jet lint --a11y  # only when explicitly requested

options.name: #A11yStrict file-level opt-in marker
options.detail: Files with #A11yStrict at the top get a11y lints; others don't. Hank can enforce it on specific modules. Very granular but obscure — beginners don't know to add it, and it requires discipline across a large team.

decisions.comparisons:
ESLint a11y:    eslint --rule jsx-a11y/...  explicit plugin; CI adds --rule flags
axe-core:       separate npm run a11y  — entirely separate tool run
Lighthouse:     CI step: lighthouse --only-categories=accessibility
SwiftUI:        XCUIAccessibilityAudit  — explicit test call in test suite
Android:        AccessibilityScanner    — separate IDE plugin, not build-time

decisions.title: Method name inside impl Type.Display
decisions.gist: What is the method name inside impl Type.Display { }?
decisions.story: Doris is building a Color type for a design tool. She wants Color to print as "rgb(255, 0, 128)" when used in string interpolation. She writes impl Color.Display { } — what method name goes inside?

options.name: fn display(self) -> String (recommended)
options.detail: Method name matches the trait name exactly. No collision with any existing Jet built-in. Reads like the trait. Consistent with how fn restore matches the Rollback trait.

options.name: fn to_string(self) -> String
options.detail: Familiar from Rust/Java/Kotlin/Swift. But to_string is a common name users already write as helpers on their own types — high collision risk. Also implies conversion, not display.

options.name: fn format(self) -> String
options.detail: Evokes string formatting but in most languages "format" means formatting with arguments/patterns. A zero-argument fn format reads as if it takes a format string.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       impl fmt::Display for Color { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter) -> fmt::Result }
Swift:      var description: String { "rgb(...)" }   // CustomStringConvertible
Python:     def __str__(self) -> str
Java:       public String toString()
Kotlin:     override fun toString(): String
Go:         func (c Color) String() string

decisions.title: Field-level marker to exclude a field from Debug auto-derive output
decisions.gist: What marker hides a sensitive field from Debug auto-derive output?
decisions.story: Walter's User struct has a password_hash and a stripe_token. He never wants these in debug output, log files, or error messages. Debug auto-derives for all structs. What annotation hides a specific field?

options.name: #[Redact] field marker (recommended)
options.detail: General-purpose privacy marker. Not just for Debug — signals that this field contains sensitive data across all serialization, logging, and display contexts. PascalCase per D-CASING1. A single marker teaches one concept: "this field is sensitive."

options.name: #[Debug.skip] field marker
options.detail: Scoped specifically to Debug output. Clear intent but introduces a new dotted-name marker form not used anywhere else in Jet. Also, a developer might want a field to be skipped in JSON too — they would then need both #[Debug.skip] and a separate serialization marker.
options.code:
struct User {
    id:            Int
    email:         String
    #[Debug.skip]
    password_hash: String   // hidden from Debug but still in JSON?
    #[Debug.skip]
    stripe_token:  String
}

options.name: No v1 field exclusion — implement Display manually to filter
options.detail: Conservative. Users who need redaction override impl Type.Display themselves. No new marker. But Debug still leaks the field — you cannot hide a field from auto-derived Debug without a language mechanism.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust:           #[allow(dead_code)]  — doesn't hide from Debug
                derive(Debug) with manual impl — only way to hide
                serde:          #[serde(skip)] / #[serde(skip_serializing)]
Python:         override __repr__ manually — no field-level annotation
Swift:          no field-level skip; override debugDescription manually
Java:           @JsonIgnore (Jackson) — serialization only, not debug
Go:             omitempty tag — JSON only

decisions.title: User-type for-loop iterable hook: beginner .each/.to_list + expert Iterable protocol
decisions.gist: Beginners iterate custom collections with .each(fn) or .to_list() — no protocol required. Experts who want `for x in mytype` without copying implement Iterable + Iterator.
decisions.story: Betty built a BTree<T> for sorted data. As a beginner she writes `bt.each(fn(val) { print(val) })` or `for val in bt.to_list()` and it just works. When she needs zero-copy in-order walks, she adds `impl BTree.Iterable` and `for val in bt` becomes native.

options.name: Beginner .each/.to_list defaults + expert Iterable hook (recommended)
options.detail: Two tiers, one path. Default: any collection exposes `.each(fn(T))` for callback iteration and `.to_list() -> [T]` when a list is needed — no trait impl, no syntax surprise. Expert opt-in: `impl Type.Iterable { fn iter(self) -> Cursor }` plus `impl Cursor.Iterator { fn next(~self) -> T? }` enables `for x in mytype` without allocating a copy. Built-in `[T]`/`Map` keep `for` natively. Custom types without the protocol never silently copy — callers choose `.each` or `.to_list()` explicitly. Matches Jet's beginner-magic / expert-control split.

options.name: impl Type.Iterator only — type is its own cursor
options.detail: Single protocol on the collection. Simpler surface but fuses collection and cursor — two simultaneous `for` loops over the same value break (shared mutable state). Rejected for the expert tier when Iterable+Iterator is the safe pattern.

options.name: Defer v1 — .to_list() / .each() only, no for-in hook
options.detail: No iterable protocol in v1. Forces copies or manual `.each` forever. Rejected now that the dual-tier design gives beginners ergonomics without obligating experts to implement anything.
options.code:
for val in bt.to_list() { print(val) }   // only path
bt.each(fn(val) { print(val) })

decisions.recommendation: Beginner `.each`/`.to_list()` out of the box; expert `impl Iterable` + `Iterator` unlocks zero-copy `for x in mytype` (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       IntoIterator + Iterator — two traits; beginners use .iter()/.into_iter()
Python:     __iter__ + __next__ — experts implement; beginners use list()
Swift:      Sequence + IteratorProtocol — same split
Kotlin:     Iterable + Iterator — for-in requires Iterable
Jet (A):    .each/.to_list() without protocol; for-in with Iterable opt-in

decisions.title: User-type square-bracket indexing: beginner .get/.set + expert Index hook
decisions.gist: Built-in List/Map keep `m[k]` out of the box. Custom types use `.get(k)` / `.set(k, v)` by default; experts who want bracket syntax implement Index (+ optional IndexMut).
decisions.story: Earl built a SparseMatrix. Beginners call `m.get(3, 7)` and `m.set(3, 7, 42.0)` — explicit, always works. When he wants `m[3, 7]` sugar, he adds `impl SparseMatrix.Index` and bracket syntax lights up.

options.name: Beginner .get/.set defaults + expert Index hook (recommended)
options.detail: Built-in `[T]` and `Map` keep native `xs[i]` / `map[k]` with no impl. User-defined types without a protocol use named `.get(k) -> V?` and `.set(k, v)` — clear, fallible, no magic. Expert opt-in: `impl Type.Index { fn get(self, k: K) -> V? }` enables `mytype[k]`; optional `impl Type.IndexMut { fn set(~self, k: K, v: V) }` enables `mytype[k] = v`. D-SIMD2's closed built-in `[]` rule stays; only user types with an explicit impl gain brackets.

options.name: impl Type.Index + IndexMut required for all indexing
options.detail: Even built-ins would route through protocols — too much ceremony for beginners. Rejected: List/Map already have blessed `[]` and should not require impl blocks.
options.code: // Would force impl on every collection type — rejected

options.name: Defer — .get/.set only forever
options.detail: No bracket hook for user types. Rejected now that the dual-tier design keeps beginners on explicit methods while experts get brackets when they want them.

decisions.recommendation: Built-in `[]` for List/Map; `.get`/`.set` for custom types by default; expert `impl Index` unlocks `mytype[k]` (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       Index/IndexMut traits — opt-in for user types; Vec has built-in []
Python:     __getitem__/__setitem__ — always protocol-based
Swift:      subscript — explicit on each type
Kotlin:     operator get/set — opt-in
Jet (A):    built-in [] for List/Map; .get/.set default; Index opt-in for experts

decisions.title: Unit construction: dot-constructor spelling, not a literal-suffix hook
decisions.gist: No new literal-suffix protocol. #UnitFamily unit types construct with dot-construction like every other Jet value: `px.{100}`, `Em.{1.5}`.
decisions.story: Hank wants typed lengths in UI styles. He should write `width: px.{100}` — same dot-constructor family as `Point.{x: 3, y: 4}` — not CSS `100px` suffixes and not a hidden coercion protocol.

options.name: Dot-constructor on unit types — no literal-suffix hook (recommended)
options.detail: Close the literal-suffix hook item. D-QUAL3 #UnitFamily already provides typed units. Construction uses the ratified dot-constructor form (D-DOTCTOR1): `px.{100}`, `Em.{1.5}`, `Pct.{50}` when the target type is known from context (`width: Px = px.{100}`). No grammar suffix, no `from_int_literal` coercion protocol, no second mechanism. Consistent with struct/enum construction everywhere else in Jet.

options.name: Bless fn from_int_literal(n: Int) -> T coercion protocol
options.detail: Context-driven implicit coercion: bare `100` routes to different unit constructors depending on inferred type. Fights I8 (one path) and hides which conversion ran. Rejected in favor of explicit `px.{100}`.

options.name: CSS-style grammar suffix `100px`
options.detail: Tier-4 grammar extension. D-EXT1 already rejected user-defined literal suffixes. Would be a second construction path beside dot-constructors.
options.code: width #= 100px   // rejected — not Jet's constructor family

decisions.recommendation: Unit values construct with dot-construction `px.{100}`; remove literal-suffix hook from card #41 (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Jet structs:  Point.{x: 3.0, y: 4.0}  — same dot-constructor family
Jet enums:    Color.Red / .Variant     — leading dot
CSS:          width: 100px            — rejected suffix grammar
Kotlin:       100.px                   — extension property, not constructor
Rust:         Px::new(100)             — function, not dot-constructor

decisions.title: Add C-style ++/-- increment and decrement operators?
decisions.gist: Jet already increments with `x += 1`. Should Jet also accept `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, and `x--` on mutable integers?
decisions.explainer: S17 ratified compound assignment (`+=`, `-=`, …) as the update-operator family. The owner asked for C-style `++`/`--`. Under I8 there should be one mechanical path — unless the owner explicitly chooses familiarity over uniformity on this site. The ballot covers full C semantics, permanent rejection, and three partial shapes (postfix-only, prefix-only, statement-only). Operand policy mirrors S17: mutable `var`, `mut` parameters, `self.field` on `mut self`, and index sites; integer types only (trap-on-overflow per D-NUMOPS2). No user-defined operator overloading.
decisions.story: Carla is porting a C sprite engine. Her game loop has `tick++` and `while (--lives > 0)` scattered through the original. She wants Jet to accept the same tokens so she can translate line-for-line, but she also wants beginners reading her code to understand what changed.

options.name: Full C-style ++/-- on mutable integer lvalues (pre + post)
options.detail: All four forms. Prefix returns the new value; postfix returns the old value. Operand must be a mutable integer lvalue (same LHS policy as S17). Applies to `Int` and sized integer widths; not `Float`. Overflow traps like `+= 1` (D-NUMOPS2). Gives C/C++ transliteration fidelity; spends a second increment spelling (I8 tension).

options.name: Reject ++/-- forever — keep `+= 1` / `-= 1` only (recommended)
options.detail: No increment/decrement operators. S17 compound assignment is the single canonical update path (I8). Matches Rust, Swift, Zig, Go, and Python. Users coming from C see a teaching error pointing at `+= 1`. Owner request is satisfied by documenting the transliteration table in the cookbook, not new syntax.

options.name: Postfix only (`x++`, `x--`) — no prefix forms
options.detail: Only postfix increment/decrement. Value of `x++` is discarded (statement form) or typed as `Void` — no old-value expression semantics. Covers the most common C loop idiom (`i++` at end of body) without prefix `--lives` in conditions. Still a second path beside `+= 1` but avoids prefix/precedence puzzles in conditions.

options.name: Prefix only (`++x`, `--x`) — no postfix forms
options.detail: Only prefix forms; they return the updated value (usable in expressions). Matches the `--lives > 0` condition pattern and `++it` iterator style. No postfix old-value trap. Rejects `tick++` at statement end — users write `tick += 1` or `++tick` there.

options.name: Statement-position only — both pre and post, never inside expressions
options.detail: Lexer/parser accept `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, `x--` only as standalone statements (or loop-header afterthought if D-LOOP-SURFACE B is extended). Using them where a value is expected is an error. Cuts the classic footgun (`arr[i] = i++`) while still letting Carla write familiar statement lines. Expression increment stays `+= 1`.

comparisons.note: Full four-form family; prefix/postfix differ in expression value. Decades of familiarity; also decades of postfix confusion.
No `++`/`--`. Updates use `+= 1`, `-= 1`, or `+=` with any step. Deliberate removal from C lineage.
No `++`/`--` (removed in Swift 3). `+= 1` / `-= 1` only.
comparisons.code:
var i = 0
i += 1

decisions.recommendation: Reject `++`/`--` (Option B). S17 already owns increment/decrement; adding C operators duplicates that job and reintroduces prefix/postfix value semantics beginners stumble on. Choose A only if C transliteration ergonomics outweigh I8 on this site.

log.text: Ballot raised from increment-operators.md plan. Five options: full C-style, reject, postfix-only, prefix-only, statement-only. Rec B on I8 + beginner clarity.

decisions.title: Should methods be ordinary functions or macro-like rewrite hooks?
decisions.gist: Keep methods as ordinary functions; use explicit hook traits for the few operations that need syntax.
decisions.explainer: Jet already ratifies methods as one structural placement for functions: inline, impl block, or external `fn Type.method(self)` all mean the same program. Treating methods as macros would blur call semantics, make refactoring up/down the hierarchy less predictable, and conflict with R11 source-fragment re-entry. The useful Jai insight is not “every method is a macro”; it is that refactoring should preserve shape and that library hooks should feel direct where the compiler blesses them.
decisions.story: Carla moves `Player.heal` from inside `struct Player` to an external method so her gameplay file reads top-down. She needs the call `p.heal(10)` to keep meaning exactly the same thing, not start participating in code rewriting because the method moved.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: “method as macro” is attractive because it can make domain APIs feel native and unlock local syntax without language work. The failure mode is worse: every method call becomes suspect, tooling cannot know whether navigation/refactor preserves behavior, and beginner code inherits a macro mental model. Jet should instead bless a tiny set of hook protocols (Iterable, Index, Display) and keep them sema-owned.

options.name: Methods are always ordinary functions (recommended)
options.detail: Inline, impl-block, and external methods are equivalent structural placements. No method can rewrite syntax or inject code. Blessed hooks remain explicit traits/protocols with sema-owned lowering.
options.code:
fn Player.heal(~self, amount: Int) { self.hp += amount }
p.heal(5)        // ordinary checked call

options.name: Compiler-known hook methods only
options.detail: Keep ordinary methods, but allow a closed list of names/traits to power syntax such as `loop x in y`, indexing, display, and future literal hooks. This is mostly current Jet law; the decision would document the boundary.

options.name: Macro methods may rewrite calls
options.detail: A method can opt into receiving call syntax and returning generated source. Powerful for DSLs, but makes method calls non-local and collides with the no-user-macros ceiling.
options.code:
#Macro fn Query.where(self, pred: Code) -> Code { ... }
users.where(.age > 18)

comparisons.note: Jai exposes broad compile-time execution and compiler message loops. It is powerful and fast for game/tool authors, but trusts project code heavily.
comparisons.code:
#run build_tables();
#modify Some_Type { /* compiler message loop territory */ }

comparisons.note: Rust keeps methods and macros separate. Proc macros generate tokens that the compiler parses and checks again.

decisions.title: What symbol family owns metadata, compiler control, and comptime splices?
decisions.gist: Use `#` for declarations/metadata, `$` only at value splice sites, and avoid `@` in new syntax.
decisions.explainer: Current Jet has converged on PascalCase `#` markers (`#Test`, `#Unsafe`, `#PubFile`, `#Ref`, `#[Codable]`) and `$name` comptime value splices. The open question is whether to split compiler-owned notes onto `@` or `$`. Physical ergonomics matters: `#` and `$` are same left-hand number row reach on US keyboards; `@` is not easier, and three marker families increase search/tooling cost. Best coherence: `#` means annotated declaration/scope/type fact, `#[...]` means multiple markers on one item, `#(...)` means effect set, and `$` means a computed compile-time value appears in runtime source.
decisions.story: Maya is exploring Jet in the LSP. She types `#` before a function and expects completions for tests, safety gates, FFI, purity, and build markers. She types `$` inside an expression and expects compile-time values, not another attribute namespace.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: `@` for compiler notes would make compiler-owned operations visually distinct and familiar to Zig users. It also creates an attractive dumping ground: `@embed`, `@run`, `@target`, `@test`, while `#` still exists for attrs. Then LSP completion and docs split across two sigils, and refactoring syntax up/down hierarchy no longer has one marker grammar. `$` as general compiler marker is worse: `$` already means splice/value, so using it for notes collapses “compute here” and “mark this item.”

options.name: One marker family: `#` metadata, `$` splice (recommended)
options.detail: Declarations, attributes, scoped gates, type facts, and compiler notes use PascalCase `#` / `#[...]`. `$` remains value splice only. No new `@` surface.

options.name: Split: `#` user attrs, `@` compiler builtins
options.detail: Rust-like attrs stay `#`; compiler operations use `@`. Distinct but less coherent and less searchable.

options.name: `$` for all compiler/comptime markers
options.detail: Make `$` the compiler/comptime family. Compact, but overloads splice sites and item markers.
options.code:
$Build fn build(b: ~Build) { ... }
$value_splice

comparisons.note: Jai leans on `#` directives for compile-time and compiler features.
comparisons.code:
#run build();
#scope_file;

comparisons.note: Zig uses `@` for compiler builtins and `comptime` as a keyword. Search is good, but `@` becomes a second namespace every user must learn.
comparisons.code:
const data = @embedFile("sprite.png");
comptime { ... }

comparisons.note: Rust uses `#[]` attributes; macros use `!`, creating a visible split between metadata and expansion.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Debug)]
println!("hi");

decisions.title: What should the first-party CLI flag API look like?
decisions.gist: Ship a typed builder/parser, not global Go-style registration.
decisions.explainer: Go’s `flag` is small and readable, but global registration fights Jet’s no-hidden-state instinct and makes tests/subcommands awkward. Jet can keep the good part: typed flags with defaults and generated help. The API should be library-level, no syntax, and usable in single-file scripts.
decisions.story: Nora writes a one-file asset packer. She wants `--input`, `--out`, and `--fast` parsed with good help text, and she wants tests to pass synthetic argv without mutating global process state.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a tiny Go clone is attractive for beginner scripts and avoids derives. But mutable global flag registries are hard to isolate in tests and conflict with modules/subcommands. A typed parser can still offer a low-ceremony builder for users who dislike markers.

options.name: Typed `#[Cli]` struct parser (recommended)
options.detail: A struct describes args; defaults and docs come from fields. Best for refactors and generated help. Requires derive/reflection machinery but no new syntax.

options.name: Go-style builder, no global registry
options.detail: Keep explicit calls but make parser an owned value for tests/subcommands.
options.code:
p := cli.Parser.new()
name #= p.string("name", default: "")
verbose #= p.bool("verbose", default: false)
p.parse(process.args())?

options.name: Go-style global flags
options.detail: Smallest call site, but hidden global state and weaker tests.
options.code:
name #= cli.string("name", "", "user name")
cli.parse()

comparisons.note: The stdlib flag package is tiny and predictable, but global registration can make larger CLIs awkward.
comparisons.code:
name := flag.String("name", "", "user name")
flag.Parse()

comparisons.note: Derive-based CLI parsing gives excellent UX but uses macro-heavy generated code.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Parser)]
struct Args { #[arg(long)] name: String }

decisions.title: Should Jet add a Jai-style `Any` for expert reflection boundaries?
decisions.gist: Do not add general `Any`; reserve typed reflection handles and `Data` trees for the real use cases.
decisions.explainer: D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 already rejects a general top type. The Jai model is useful as an implementation technique for reflection, plugin ABI, debugger values, and format trees, but exposing it as an ordinary parameter type would punch a hole through static typing. If Jet needs this power, it should appear as a narrow expert/runtime handle with no implicit conversions.
decisions.story: Owen writes an inspector panel for game entities. He wants to show arbitrary field values in tooling, but his gameplay APIs should still say `Health`, `Position`, or `Inventory`, not `Any`.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: rejecting `Any` too hard can make editor tooling, serialization bridges, and plugin ABIs clumsy. The answer is not a universal type; it is a closed set of reflective value handles whose operations are checked and whose construction sites are controlled by compiler/reflection APIs.

options.name: Keep no general `Any`; use reflection/Data handles (recommended)
options.detail: D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 stands. Tooling gets `reflect.Value` / `DataTree`; app APIs stay statically typed.
options.code: fn render_debug(v: reflect.Value) { print(v.type_name()) }

options.name: Expert-gated `core.reflect.Any` handle only
options.detail: Expose a library type with type info + pointer for reflection internals. No implicit conversion from all values; construction requires reflection/comptime APIs or unsafe gate.
options.code:
use core.reflect
fn inspect(a: reflect.Any) { ... }

options.name: General `Any` top type
options.detail: Any value can flow into `Any`. Ergonomic for dynamic code, but weakens the type system and repeats problems D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 closed.
options.code: fn log(x: Any) { print(x) }

comparisons.note: Any is a type-info pointer plus value pointer. Useful for tooling/reflection, but weakens static guarantees if ordinary APIs accept it.
comparisons.code: Any :: struct { type: *Type_Info; value_pointer: *void; }

comparisons.note: `Any` exists, but serious APIs prefer protocols/generics/enums to recover static meaning.
comparisons.code: func log(_ value: Any) { print(value) }

decisions.title: Should Jet adopt Jai-style dynamic-array type syntax?
decisions.gist: Keep `[T]` for dynamic lists and `[T#N]` for fixed-size lists; do not add `[..]$T`.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has one compact collection family: `[T]` dynamic list, `[K,V]` map, `[T#N]` fixed-size list. Jai’s `[..]T` is clear in Jai because its array family differs. In Jet, adding `[..]$Type` would collide visually with ranges, splices, and existing list type grammar while creating a second dynamic-list spelling.
decisions.story: Iris ports a Jai particle system. She sees `particles: [..]$Particle` and asks for the Jet equivalent. The safest answer is a direct transliteration table, not new syntax.
decisions.inWild:
particles: [Particle] := []
particles.push(Particle.{ pos: .{0, 0}, vel: .{1, 0} })

ids: [Int#128] := fixed_ids()
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: `[..]T` distinguishes slice/dynamic/fixed arrays well in languages with multiple array kinds. Jet should still resist because `..` already means inclusive range and `step`, `$` means comptime splice, and `[T]` is shorter and beginner-obvious.

options.name: Keep current `[T]` / `[T#N]` family (recommended)
options.detail: One dynamic-list spelling. Porting docs map Jai `[..]T` to Jet `[T]`.

options.name: Add `[..]T` as dynamic-list spelling
options.detail: Jai familiarity, but duplicate semantics and range visual overload.
options.code: items: [..]Entity := []

options.name: Reserve `[..]T` for slices/views later
options.detail: Do not use it for owning dynamic arrays; keep it available if slice syntax needs it.
options.code: view: [..]U8 = bytes.slice(0..16)

comparisons.note: Dynamic-array type uses a compact bracket marker distinct from fixed arrays.
comparisons.code: items: [..]Entity;

comparisons.note: Slices are `[]T`; fixed arrays are `[N]T`; capacity-owning collections are library types.
comparisons.code:
var slice: []u8 = buffer[0..];
var fixed: [16]u8 = undefined;

decisions.title: Should Jet add a Jai-style `shift` primitive for stream parsers?
decisions.gist: Add library cursor/reader methods if needed; do not add a new language operator.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s shift style is useful for binary parsers and arena/cursor code: consume bytes/items from the front while advancing a pointer. In Jet this should live as explicit methods on cursor/reader types (`read_u32`, `take`, `advance`) so ownership and bounds checks remain visible.
decisions.story: Sam writes a binary asset loader. He wants compact code that consumes a header, count, and payload from a byte buffer without hand-managing indices.
decisions.inWild:
cursor := bytes.cursor()
magic #= cursor.read_u32_le()?
count #= cursor.read_u16_le()?
items #= cursor.take(count)?
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a dedicated `shift` token could make parser code beautiful. It would also be domain-specific syntax competing with method calls and `?`, while hiding failure/bounds behavior. Method names preserve autocomplete and diagnostics.

options.name: Library cursor methods only (recommended)
options.detail: Add/standardize `cursor.read_*`, `take`, `advance`, and `remaining`; no syntax.
options.code:
id #= c.read_u32_le()?
name #= c.read_text(len)?

options.name: Builtin `shift<T>(cursor)` function
options.detail: A first-party generic helper, still ordinary function syntax.
options.code: id #= shift<U32>(~c)?

options.name: New shift operator/keyword
options.detail: Most compact, least general; adds language surface for one parser idiom.
options.code: id #= shift U32 from c

comparisons.note: Shift-style helpers make parsers compact by advancing a pointer/cursor as data is read.
comparisons.code: value := shift *u32, *cursor;

comparisons.note: Byte readers usually expose methods that advance internal position and return Results.
comparisons.code: let n = cursor.read_u32::<LittleEndian>()?;

decisions.title: Should Jet support compact pointer-cast/deref chains like Jai?
decisions.gist: Keep casts and deref explicit inside `#Unsafe`; add docs for the Jai transliteration.
decisions.explainer: The Jai expression means: take a stored untyped pointer, cast it to pointer-to-bool, then dereference it. Jet already has raw pointer `*T` and postfix `p.*` under `#Unsafe`. The question is whether to add a compact cast/deref chain for reflection internals. Safety priority says no: every untyped pointer cast should be loud and gated.
decisions.story: Priya is implementing a debugger variable editor. A reflected slot tells her a field is Bool and gives a raw pointer. She needs to set the field, but only in audited tooling code.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: Jai’s chain is very readable to experts once learned and great in metaprogramming code. In Jet, the same compactness would normalize untyped pointer mutation. Keep it explicit, and make reflection APIs provide typed setters where possible so most code never casts.

options.name: Explicit cast + postfix deref inside `#Unsafe` (recommended)
options.detail: Current low-level model. Add docs/examples, not syntax.

options.name: Typed reflection setter API
options.detail: Avoid pointer syntax at call site; reflection library checks type before mutation.
options.code: slot.set_bool(true)?

options.name: Jai-style cast/deref chain
options.detail: Compact expert syntax, but hides two unsafe operations in one expression.
options.code: slot.value_pointer.(*Bool).* = true

comparisons.note: Type-info + pointer casts can be compact and expressive for reflection internals.
comparisons.code: slot.var.value_pointer.(*bool).* = true;

comparisons.note: Raw pointer casts and dereferences are inside explicit unsafe blocks.
comparisons.code: unsafe { *(ptr as *mut bool) = true; }

decisions.title: What spelling should visible uninitialized storage use?
decisions.gist: Prefer explicit `#Uninit` marker over punctuation sentinel `---`.
decisions.explainer: Visible uninit is expert-tier storage control: allocate a slot now, prove it is written before read. A punctuation sentinel is terse and Jai-familiar, but easy to skim past and physically awkward enough to invite typos (`--`, em dash, minus chains). A PascalCase marker fits Jet’s existing audit/metadata family and LSP completion.
decisions.story: Leah fills a fixed buffer from a device packet. She needs storage before all fields are known, but she wants the compiler to reject any read before assignment.
decisions.inWild:
#Uninit header: PacketHeader
header.magic = cursor.read_u32_le()?
header.len = cursor.read_u16_le()?
process(header)
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: `---` has excellent Jai muscle memory and visually says “hole”. But Jet’s marker family is searchable (`#Uninit`), teachable, and composable with lints/docs. Physical ergonomics: three hyphens are easy keys but create visual noise near `->`, `--`, `-=`, ranges, and comments.

options.name: `#Uninit name: Type` marker (recommended)
options.detail: Searchable, LSP-completable, consistent with expert markers. Reads as an audited storage state.
options.code:
#Uninit packet: Packet
packet.id = id

options.name: Jai-style `name: Type := ---`
options.detail: Compact expression-style sentinel. Adds a punctuation literal with no value semantics.
options.code:
packet: Packet := ---
packet.id = id

options.name: Library wrapper `Uninit<T>`
options.detail: Very explicit, but noisier and less beginner-friendly diagnostics.
options.code:
packet := Uninit<Packet>.new()
packet.write(Packet.{ id })

comparisons.note: `---` means intentionally uninitialized. Very terse, but punctuation-heavy.
comparisons.code: header: Packet_Header = ---;

comparisons.note: `undefined` is explicit but keyword-like and can leak into ordinary code.
comparisons.code: var header: Header = undefined;

comparisons.note: `MaybeUninit<T>` is library-explicit and unsafe to assume initialized.
comparisons.code: let mut x = MaybeUninit::<Header>::uninit();

decisions.title: Should stored-reference fields use `#Ref(Label)` or capability-style `~Type`?
decisions.gist: Keep `#Ref(Label)` for stored owner relationships; `~T` stays call-time edit access.
decisions.explainer: `~T` already means exclusive mutable access for a parameter/call capability. A stored reference field is a different fact: this field points into some owner value, and sema must track that owner relationship by label. Reusing `~T` would conflate “may edit during this call” with “stored borrow tied to owner”. That breaks Jet’s one-mechanism rule even though it looks shorter.
decisions.story: Earl stores token text as a view into an arena-owned source buffer. The field is not “mutable access to String”; it is “this String view belongs to source”.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: `field: ~T` is physically easy and reuses a known sigil. But `~` is already a call-site/parameter capability and is hard to hit on many keyboards. More importantly, stored refs need a label (`source`, `arena`, `owner`) or diagnostics cannot explain what must outlive what. `#Ref(source)` is longer because it carries the missing semantic fact.

options.name: Keep `#Ref(Label) field: T` (recommended)
options.detail: Label names the owner relationship; marker stays in metadata family; no conflict with call-time `~T`.
options.code: struct Slice { #Ref(buffer) bytes: [U8] }

options.name: Use `field: ~T` for stored refs
options.detail: Short, but conflicts with `~T` edit capability and loses owner label unless another syntax is added.
options.code: struct Slice { bytes: ~[U8] }

options.name: Use `field: &T` for stored shared refs
options.detail: Familiar to Rust users, but Jet already uses `&T` for share/escape capability and still lacks owner label.
options.code: struct Slice { bytes: &[U8] }

comparisons.note: Stored references name a lifetime relationship; mutable access is a separate `&mut` concept.
comparisons.code:
struct View<'a> { text: &'a str }
fn edit(x: &mut String) {}

comparisons.note: Borrowing/consuming annotations are access-mode concepts, separate from object storage identity.
comparisons.code: borrowing value / consuming value

decisions.title: What is Jet’s compile-time build entrypoint?
decisions.gist: Give Jet a build-time main: one explicit `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`, selected by the build surface.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s `#run` is powerful because build code is just language code. Jet should import that power through a single auditable entrypoint instead of hidden module-level execution. Local `comptime {}` remains for value computation; the build entrypoint owns graph construction: targets, generated source, assets, toolchains, profiles, and package/workspace integration. Generated source still re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema (R11).
decisions.story: Marcus is building a game. He wants to pack textures, generate an enum from asset names, compile shaders, and then build the game binary with one command. His studio security team wants the same build to explain exactly what ran and what files/network endpoints it touched.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a build-time main can become Cargo build.rs with better syntax: dependency code executes before users inspect it. Patch: one selected root entrypoint, `BuildContext` authority only, D-CTEFFECT1 tiers, dependency Tier 2 denied by default, generated-source re-check, lock/provenance, and `jet explain-build`. Do not let every imported module have hidden build hooks.

options.name: `Build.entry` selects `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?` (recommended)
options.detail: One explicit build-time main. The marker makes the authority boundary visible; `Build.entry` makes selection explicit for tools and CI. Local `comptime {}` remains separate.

options.name: Magic `fn build()` discovered by name
options.detail: Lower ceremony and Jai/Zig-like, but less explicit for auditors and creates name magic beside runtime `main`.
options.code:
fn build(ctx: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ? { ... }
// driver auto-discovers by name

options.name: `comptime main` in any module
options.detail: Maximal #run feel. Rejected unless owner accepts hidden import-time execution risk.
options.code: comptime fn main(ctx: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ? { ... }

options.name: No build entrypoint; only declarative `Build.{}` plus local `comptime {}`
options.detail: Safest and easiest to audit, but cannot replace Jai/Zig/Make-class orchestration.
options.code: build: Build.{ sources: ["src/main.jet"] }

comparisons.note: `#run` can execute arbitrary compile-time code and participate in build orchestration. It is fun and direct, but authority is broad by default.
comparisons.code:
Texture_Info :: #run build_texture_table();
#run { build_game(); }

comparisons.note: `build.zig` is a programmatic build file with explicit steps. Strong model, but separate from ordinary source entrypoints.
`build.rs` runs before compilation and communicates through files/env instructions. Powerful but stringly and historically easy to abuse.
comparisons.code: fn main() { println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=schema.json"); }

decisions.title: What authority does build-time code get by default?
decisions.gist: Build code gets pure and locked reproducible inputs by default; ambient effects require source audit plus policy.
decisions.explainer: Build metaprogramming is supply-chain code execution. Jet needs a policy model that is fun locally but enforceable in CI and enterprises. D-CTEFFECT1 gives the effect tiers; this decision fixes the build-system default: root builds may request authority, dependencies are denied ambient authority unless project/org policy grants it, and every granted capability is recorded in lock/provenance.
decisions.story: Alicia maintains a fintech service. She is fine with a root build script reading `schema/*.sql`, but she cannot allow a transitive dependency to read CI secrets or hit the network during build.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: too much policy can make game-dev builds feel bureaucratic. Too little policy loses enterprise adoption. The compromise is profile-sensitive: developer default allows pure + locked Tier 1 and prompts for Tier 2; CI strict/offline deny drift; enterprise can allowlist roots/domains/tools. The model must not rely on wrapper scripts.

options.name: Tiered policy with `BuildContext` authority only (recommended)
options.detail: Pure + locked Tier 1 by default. Tier 2 needs `#Impure("reason")`, CLI/project/org permission, and provenance. Dependencies get no Tier 2 unless explicitly granted.
options.code:
jet build --profile=ci --locked --deny-impure
jet audit-effects

options.name: Warn-only policy for impure build effects
options.detail: Fast and friendly, but CI can accidentally ship non-reproducible builds.
options.code: Warning [L3102]: build reads `$HOME/.token`

options.name: Pure-only build code
options.detail: Maximum reproducibility, but blocks shader compilation, bindgen, asset packing, and real-world package builds.
options.code: // ctx.exec, env, unpinned network: always errors

options.name: Jai-style unrestricted build execution
options.detail: Most fun and powerful locally; unacceptable supply-chain default for Jet.
options.code: #run { run_process("curl https://...") }

comparisons.note: Builds are sandboxed and inputs are explicit; reproducibility is excellent but general programming ergonomics are specialized.
comparisons.code: derivation { src = ./src; buildInputs = [ openssl ]; }

comparisons.note: Actions declare inputs/outputs and remote cache keys. Strong enterprise model; BUILD language is separate from app language.
comparisons.code: genrule(name = "schema", srcs = ["schema.sql"], outs = ["db.rs"], cmd = "...")

comparisons.note: Build scripts are easy but broad; policy/audit is mostly convention and sandboxing is external.
comparisons.code: fn main() { std::process::Command::new("cc").spawn().unwrap(); }

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in tools/Tower/docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.
